officers.name: David Eyler
officers.note: Eyler chaired the seven-member Judicial Committee of Associated Students in 1970-71. The yearbook says the committee interpreted the A.S. constitution, heard appeals of all election disputes, ruled on student traffic violations and considered questions of student conduct referred to it by the Dean of Student Affairs.
profile: David Eyler chaired Associated Students' seven-member Judicial Committee in 1970-71. Per the 1971 Talisman's Associated Students section, the committee interpreted the Associated Students constitution, heard appeals of election disputes, ruled on student traffic violations, and considered questions of student conduct referred to it by the Dean of Student Affairs. The yearbook's group photograph names Eyler as chairman, with Michael E. Freville as vice-chairman, Linda Jones as secretary, and Sam DeShazer, Jeanne Jackson, Brad Coffman, Mark Barber and Pat Riley also on the committee.
No further record of Eyler's term survives in this archive.

officers.name: Michael E. Freville
officers.note: Freville was vice-chairman of the Judicial Committee in 1970-71. The committee's group photograph caption prints his office beside his name. The volume's senior section also lists him with Associated Students and the Judicial Council, without giving an office.
profile: Michael E. Freville was vice-chairman of Associated Students' Judicial Committee in 1970-71, alongside chairman David Eyler. The 1971 Talisman's committee photograph caption names his office, and the volume's senior portraits list him separately with Associated Students and the Judicial Council, without specifying an office there.
No further record of Freville's term survives in this archive.

officers.name: Linda Jones
officers.note: Jones was secretary of the Judicial Committee in 1970-71. The volume does not say whether she is the Linda Jones elected Associated Students president in April 1971, and this archive should not merge the two names without a source that connects them.
profile: Linda Jones is listed as secretary of the Judicial Committee in the 1971 Talisman's Associated Students section, serving under committee chairman David Eyler and vice-chairman Michael E. Freville, in the same year that Carol Gray held the separately elected office of ASG secretary. A different Linda Jones was elected Associated Students president in April 1971, but the archive holds no source connecting the two, and this record does not merge them.

members.name: Tony Cochran
members.note: A 1973 Talisman profile records Cochran as a representative-at-large who roomed with Doug Alexander, his fraternity big brother and vice president of student government, and says he learned from Alexander and from president John Lyne. That pairing matches the 1971 Talisman's independent record of the 1970-71 executive, Lyne as president and Alexander as vice president, which is why the term is placed here. The same profile records him as a Sigma Nu chapter president and national Man of the Year, and as the son of the late Robert G. Cochran, dean of public affairs and public relations. A Herald report of an October 1970 primary would date the election precisely; the archive has not read it.
profile: Cochran served as a representative at large in the 1970-71 Associated Students Congress, rooming at the time with his fraternity big brother Doug Alexander, the sitting vice president, and crediting what he learned from Alexander and from president John Lyne; he said that the next year he worked with Linda Jones and Joe Glasser. A 1973 Talisman profile, occasioned by his selection as Sigma Nu's national Man of the Year, said he had also been president of the fraternity's chapter and, the profile said, its scholar for three years; it named him commander of WKU's ROTC program the year before, where he produced a training film about the program that the Army paid to have copied and shown around the country. He was the son of Robert G. Cochran, the university's dean of public affairs and public relations, who had died by the time the profile ran.

members.name: Joe Gerard
members.seat: member elected from Congress to the Executive Council
members.note: Named in the same Executive Council caption as one of the three members elected from Congress.
profile: Gerard was one of three Congress members elected to the Executive Council for 1970-71, serving alongside Peggy Hundley and Glen Sweet under president John Lyne and vice president Doug Alexander. The council's role, as the Talisman described it, was to weigh policy and proposals before they reached the full Congress.

members.name: Peggy Hundley
members.seat: member elected from Congress to the Executive Council
members.note: The volume describes the Executive Council as the four executive officers plus three members elected from Congress; Hundley is one of the three named in the photograph caption.
profile: Hundley was one of three Congress members elected to the Executive Council for 1970-71, serving alongside Joe Gerard and Glen Sweet under president John Lyne and vice president Doug Alexander. The council's role, as the Talisman described it, was to weigh policy and proposals before they reached the full Congress.

members.name: Ben Allen Burns, Jr.
members.note: The 1971 Talisman's senior directory lists him in the Associated Students Congress alongside the Interfraternity Council presidency, cheerleading, Alpha Gamma Rho and the Cherry Country Life Club. He was a senior in 1970-71; the directory does not date the Congress term.
profile: Burns sat in the Associated Students Congress at some point during his time at Western, according to the Talisman's senior directory, compiled for his senior year of 1970-71, which also lists him as president of the Interfraternity Council and a member of the cheerleading squad, Alpha Gamma Rho and the Cherry Country Life Club. The directory does not date his Congress term.

members.name: Pamela Adele King
members.note: The 1971 Talisman's senior directory lists her in the Associated Students Congress and on the Academic Council, alongside Kappa Delta, Phi Upsilon Omicron, the Crescent Club of Lambda Chi Alpha and the honors programme. She was a senior in 1970-71; the directory does not date the Congress term.
profile: King sat in the Associated Students Congress and on the Academic Council at some point during her time at Western, according to the Talisman's senior directory, compiled for her senior year of 1970-71, which also lists her in Kappa Delta, Phi Upsilon Omicron, the Crescent Club of Lambda Chi Alpha and the honors programme. The directory does not date either term.

members.name: Martha Townley Lamason
members.note: The 1971 Talisman's senior directory lists her in the Congress of Associated Students and as junior class representative-at-large, side by side but undated and not stated to be the same office. She was a senior in 1970-71, so the junior-class title would ordinarily date to 1969-70; the Congress service itself is undated.
profile: Lamason sat in the Congress of Associated Students at some point during her time at Western, according to the Talisman's senior directory, compiled for her senior year of 1970-71, which also records her as junior-class representative at large, a title that would ordinarily have been held the year before, in 1969-70. The directory dates neither role, and it does not say whether the class-representative title and the Congress seat were the same office.

members.name: Patricia B. McEwen
members.note: The 1971 Talisman's senior directory lists her in the Associated Students Congress, with Alpha Delta Pi and Panhellenic. She was a senior in 1970-71; the directory does not date the Congress term.
profile: McEwen sat in the Associated Students Congress at some point during her time at Western, according to the Talisman's senior directory, compiled for her senior year of 1970-71, which also lists her in Alpha Delta Pi and Panhellenic. The directory does not date her Congress term.

members.name: Glen Sweet
members.seat: member elected from Congress to the Executive Council
members.note: Named in the same Executive Council caption as one of the three members elected from Congress.
profile: Sweet was one of three Congress members elected to the Executive Council for 1970-71, serving alongside Joe Gerard and Peggy Hundley under president John Lyne and vice president Doug Alexander. The council's role, as the Talisman described it, was to weigh policy and proposals before they reached the full Congress.

members.name: Sally Ann Webb
members.note: The 1971 Talisman's senior directory lists her in the Associated Students Congress, with Panhellenic, Ilva Scott, dorm council and Alpha Xi Delta, and a profile in the same volume says she had served on the Congress. She was a senior in 1970-71 and a past president of the Panhellenic Council; the directory covers her whole career at Western and does not date the Congress term.

src.label: 1971 Talisman, senior directory and profile, pp. 95, 132

profile: Webb sat in the Associated Students Congress at some point during her time at Western, according to the Talisman's senior directory and a companion profile covering her senior year, 1970-71. The profile centers on her tenure as past president of the Panhellenic Council - "I'm gung-ho Greeks," she told the Talisman, pushing back on the idea that sorority members had to fit a stereotype - and does not separately date her Congress service.

leaders.name: Linda Jones
leaders.note: First woman to hold the office. The WKU Timeline dates her election to 6 April 1971, matching the plaque year. The Herald of 28 April 1972 carries a piece headed 'Jones, Linda. Reflects on Term' in the same issue as a strike call over dorm visitation.

sources.label: WKU SGA, Former SGA Presidents roster, archived 24 Sep 2001

profile: Jones was elected the first woman president of the Associated Student Government on 6 April 1971; the Western Alumnus photographed her being sworn in with faculty regent Lowell Harrison by Georgia Bates.

That fall, on 14 September 1971, the Herald reported the Associated Students affiliating with a wider student association, though the article index alone does not identify which body. By 1 February 1972, four years after the student regent seat was created, the Herald was still reporting the seat had no vote.

Through February and March 1972, Jones's Congress pushed a rewritten constitution: it voted section by section on 22 February, when the Herald printed the executive branch's full text, and the Herald reported the executive branch accepted on 29 February. The same 29 February issue reported the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union planning court action connected to Associated Students and The Fly, a separate WKU underground newspaper, and carried Jones's own piece, 'Associated Students Corrects Herald', a public correction of the paper's coverage of the organization. The archive does not yet hold the text of either the KCLU piece or Jones's correction, so the underlying dispute and what she corrected both remain unconfirmed.

Days earlier, the Herald's 25 February 1972 issue ran under the headline 'Chaos Reigns at Associated Students Meeting', alongside a separate piece arguing that student interest in the organization had collapsed and the Associated Students had followed it down.

The constitution went to referendum at the end of March: the Herald's 28 March issue urged students to 'Vote Yes' ahead of a two-day vote, and Associated Students formally endorsed the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union's lawsuit in the same issue. The archive does not yet show the referendum's result or turnout.

Her term closed on 28 April 1972 as a Mass Action Committee called for a strike over dorm visitation and the Associated Students installed its next officers; the same issue reported students had won six votes on a university council, and carried Jones's own reflection on her year in office.

events.title: Linda Jones elected first woman ASG president
events.body: Jones became the first woman elected president of the Associated Student Government. A photograph in the Western Alumnus shows her being sworn in alongside faculty regent Lowell Harrison by Georgia Bates.

events.title: Associated Students affiliates with a wider student association
events.body: An early attempt to gain leverage beyond the Hill. Which body it joined is not clear from the article index alone.

events.title: 'Student Regent May Get Vote'
events.body: Four years after the seat was created it was still non-voting. The same issue has the Academic Council clarifying grievance procedure and an Associated Students open session scheduled for 12 February.

events.title: 'Chaos Reigns at Associated Students Meeting'
events.body: The same issue carries students planning a petition to force dorm visitation and a separate piece arguing student interest had collapsed and the Associated Students had followed it down.

events.title: Congress votes on a section of the new constitution; full text published
events.body: The Associated Students Congress voted on a section of the proposed constitution, and the Herald printed the full text of the document's proposed executive branch alongside the vote coverage.

events.title: Executive branch of a revised constitution accepted
events.body: The Herald reported acceptance of the executive branch of a revised Associated Students constitution. The archive does not yet hold the article's text or what changed.

events.title: Kentucky Civil Liberties Union plans court action on behalf of Associated Students
events.body: The Herald reported the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union planning court action on behalf of Associated Students, under a headline that also named The Fly, a separate WKU underground newspaper active that year. The archive does not yet hold the article's text, so the underlying dispute is not yet confirmed.

events.title: Linda Jones publicly corrects the Herald
events.body: President Linda Jones wrote a piece headlined 'Associated Students Corrects Herald', a public correction of the paper's own reporting on the organization. The archive does not yet hold the article's text or what it corrected.

events.title: 'Vote Yes' campaign for the new constitution; referendum set
events.body: The Herald carried a piece by Nancy Pape urging students to 'Vote Yes' on the Associated Students constitution ahead of a referendum set for the next two days, in the same issue that advertised an Associated Students mini-concert.

events.title: Associated Students endorses the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union lawsuit
events.body: The Herald reported that Associated Students formally endorsed the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union's lawsuit, a month after the Herald first reported the union planning court action connected to the organization and The Fly.

events.title: A strike threat over visitation, and six votes won on a university council
events.body: A Mass Action Committee called for a strike over dorm visitation while the Associated Students installed next year's officers. Buried in the same issue: students gained six votes on a university council. Linda Jones reflected on her term.

events.title: The Trinidad Steel Band and the Serendipity Singers
events.body: The Herald previewed the double bill on 14 September as "Folk Rock vs Steel Band in Thursday Concert" and Kim Weaver's review on 21 September was headed "Steel Band Betters Singers in Concert." The 1972 Talisman calls it the first major Associated Students sponsored concert of the year and says student requests had brought the steel band back for a second consecutive year.

events.title: Benjamin Spock, the first Associated Students speaker of the year
events.body: The Herald of 21 September announced Dr Benjamin Spock lecturing on campus that Thursday. The 1972 Talisman records that Spock, the first speaker sponsored by the Associated Students that year, attacked the United States role in Vietnam and drew a crowd of about 1,100.

events.title: Ike and Tina Turner headline Homecoming before about 12,000
events.body: The 1972 Talisman reports the Ike and Tina Turner Revue performing before an estimated crowd of 12,000 in Diddle Arena at the Homecoming concert, backed by the eight-member Kings of Rhythm. The Herald of 19 October ran "Concert Lovers Buoyed by Turnout for Ike & Tina Turner" alongside a letter from Phyllis Sower repulsed at the actions of a student at the Friday night concert. It was the high point of the Associated Students' concert year.
events.money: estimated crowd of 12,000 in Diddle Arena

events.title: A mock election for governor draws 1,175 votes
events.body: The Associated Students ran a mock gubernatorial election on 21 October 1971. The 1972 Talisman records that only 1,175 of Western's 11,000 students voted and that they elected the Republican Tom Emberton; the Herald reported the result on 22 October. Kentucky's voters chose Wendell Ford by a substantial margin on 2 November.

events.title: First Gear plays a mini-concert
events.body: The Herald of 22 October reported First Gear featured for a mini-concert. The 1972 Talisman shows Larnelle Harris of First Gear on stage at an Associated Students sponsored mini-concert; the Persuasions and Supa were among the other groups that autumn.

events.title: Supa brings a jamboree to Western
events.body: The Herald announced on 29 October that the Associated Students had set a mini-concert with Supa for the next day, and Roger Miller's review on 2 November was headed "Mini-Concert Doesn't Mean Mini-Talent." A letter from Brent Ferguson the same week praised the Associated Students mini-concerts.

events.title: The government goes after rock groups
events.body: Travis Witt reported in the Herald that the Associated Students were contacting rock groups. The 1972 Talisman names Leon Russell, Mountain, Alice Cooper and It's a Beautiful Day as the acts approached after students asked for bigger names.

events.title: Mountain and Black Oak Arkansas cancelled the day before the show
events.body: The Herald billed two rock groups for a 2 December Associated Students concert on 12 November and named Mountain and Black Oak Arkansas on 19 November. The 1972 Talisman records that on 2 December, the day before the engagement, student government leaders were forced to cancel because Mountain's lead singer Felix Pappalardi was ill. A letter from Terry Gatlin questioning the cancellation ran in the Herald of 10 December.

events.title: A surprise mini-concert with Friction
events.body: Roger Miller reported in the Herald that a surprise mini-concert on the Wednesday had hot music by Friction. It came the week after the Mountain and Black Oak Arkansas cancellation.

events.title: The Legal Rights Committee runs a symposium with lawyers
events.body: Stephanie Madison reported that the Associated Students Legal Rights Committee was planning a symposium with lawyers for 1 December. Carter Pence's report on 3 December, "Students Air Complaints at Symposium," covered the event.

events.title: The Cellar, the Associated Students teahouse, opens
events.body: Roger Miller announced the opening in the Herald under the headline "Another First: the Cellar, Associated Students Teahouse, Opens Friday." The paper covered it again a week later as "Cellar-Dwellers" and reported the campus teahouse stirred mixed emotions; by the end of April the Herald was calling it a dimly lit teahouse that outshone the government's other efforts. The 1972 Talisman describes it as a coffee house in West Hall.

events.title: A free calendar for students
events.body: The Herald reported that the Associated Students were offering a free calendar, and Joe Huggins announced it again on 21 January. The same issue reported the government scheduling lectures, concerts and a film series for the second semester.

events.title: Art Buchwald lectures
events.body: Roger Miller reported that the humour columnist Art Buchwald would lecture that night. The 1972 Talisman records his lecture as "Art Buchwald at Large" and says it combined personal anecdotes with political commentary; he stayed afterwards to talk with students.

events.title: James J. Kilpatrick speaks
events.body: Reginald Glass announced in the Herald that the syndicated columnist James J. Kilpatrick would speak that night. The 1972 Talisman records him describing the youth vote as a real problem for the Republicans.

events.title: The Associated Students movie series opens with King Kong
events.body: The Herald announced that the Associated Students movie series would open the next day with "King Kong," and an editorial three days later said the series could be a hit. The 1972 Talisman lists the Gaslight film series among the government's new entertainment; the Herald of 2 May had W. C. Fields in "The Flying Ace" set for Gaslight.

events.title: The Jake Jones mini-concert is cancelled
events.body: The Herald reported that the Associated Students had cancelled the Jake Jones mini-concert set for 29 January. The same issue carried a letter from Anthony Kinzel disconcerted with the government.

events.title: A cancelled Lennon and Ono screening brings a furious postbag
events.body: The Herald of 28 January had announced John Lennon and Yoko Ono films for the following week. On 4 February the paper printed three letters about the cancellation, one from a student who wanted to see the Lennon film and two headed "Disappointed at Film Cancellation" and "Furious at Film Cancellation," alongside Roger Miller reporting the Associated Students Congress reacting to censorship.

events.title: Norman Mailer lectures
events.body: Roger Miller announced in the Herald of 8 February that Norman Mailer's lecture was slated for the following night. The 1972 Talisman records the author and social critic telling his audience that amateurism was replacing professionalism.

events.title: Four sent to the entertainment conference
events.body: Jill Flanders reported that Reginald Glass, Mike Fiorella, Ron Beck and Jim Schmidt attended an entertainment conference. The 1972 Talisman explains the machinery behind the year's programme: Ron Beck was unit co-ordinator for the state branch of the National Entertainment Conference, ten schools were represented, the state body met on the Western campus in both semesters for programming workshops, and the three mini-concerts each semester were the result.

events.title: The Isaac Hayes concert is cancelled
events.body: Carter Pence reported the cancellation in the Herald of 18 February. The 1972 Talisman says the 17 February concert failed to materialise because Hayes was suffering from flu, and that he later contacted Western to reschedule.

events.title: Benjamin Mays on two decades of human rights
events.body: The Herald announced the black educator's lecture on 25 February and ran "Benjamin Mays Speaks Tonight" on 29 February. The 1972 Talisman gives his subject as "Two Decades of Human Rights"; the yearbook's caption says he spoke on 29 February while its running text says only that he was scheduled to.

events.title: Edwin Reischauer, former ambassador to Japan
events.body: The Herald announced that the former ambassador would speak that night. The same issue reported that the Associated Students would present "The Fantasticks" and carried an editorial headed "Herald Salutes Associated Students."

events.title: The Imperials play a mini-concert
events.body: The Herald of 11 April announced that the Thursday Associated Students mini-concert would feature the Imperials.

events.title: The Carpenters in Diddle Arena
events.body: The Herald of 14 April announced that the Carpenters would appear in concert the following Tuesday. The 1972 Talisman confirms the brother and sister recording act appeared in Diddle Arena on 18 April; they had been promised to students back in October alongside Mountain, Black Oak Arkansas and Isaac Hayes.

events.title: It's a Beautiful Day and If close the concert year
events.body: The Herald of 20 April announced a rock concert for the following Thursday with It's a Beautiful Day and If. Reginald Glass wrote the preview "Beautiful Day, If Headline Concert" in the issue of 25 April.

events.title: The Cellar finishes the year the best thing the government did
events.body: The Herald of 28 April reported the Cellar's finals were set and ran a piece headed "Cellar: It's Only a Dimly Lit Teahouse but Outshines Other Associated Student Government Efforts." The same issue reported a concert highlighting the Folk Arts Festival and the installation of next year's officers.

events.title: Finances and scheduling name the problem
events.body: The Herald ran a piece headed "Finances, Scheduling Pose Problems in Entertainment" in the week of Homecoming. Over the following month the paper printed an editorial arguing the benefits outweighed the risks in scheduling big concerts and letters from students wanting bigger concerts and disputing the paper's handling of the entertainment question.

events.title: Reginald Glass signs the Associated Students' entertainment contracts
events.body: The 1972 Talisman photographed Reginald Glass, vice-president of Associated Students, signing a speaker contract, and said signing contracts for concerts and speakers was one of his responsibilities. The first speaker the Associated Students sponsored was Dr Benjamin Spock. Its other activities that year included bringing in the Trinidad Steel Band, Ike and Tina Turner and several mini-concerts, sponsoring the Homecoming dance, and running a mock election before the Kentucky governor's race.

events.title: The Emme Kemp Jazz Trio opens the ASG mini-concert season
events.body: The Herald reported on 31 August 1971 that the Kemp Trio had set a concert. The 1972 Talisman recorded that the Associated Students entertained students with several mini-concerts that fall semester, small-scale shows meant to give top quality entertainment at less cost and presented in cooperation with other Kentucky colleges, and that the season started with the Emme Kemp Jazz Trio; student requests then brought the Trinidad Steel Band back with the Serendipity Singers.

events.title: Associated Students rescheduled the Isaac Hayes concert
events.body: The Isaac Hayes concert set for 17 February 1972 fell through when Hayes had flu, and the 1972 Talisman records that Associated Students rescheduled it for 23 March. Stephanie Madison's review in the Herald of 28 March shows the rescheduled show went ahead.

events.title: The year's programme summed up in the yearbook
events.body: The 1972 Talisman summarised Linda Jones's year under the heading "A.S. makes great strides in implementing new programs": in entertainment, mini-concerts, a coffee house in West Hall and the Gaslight film series joined several top-name musical groups and lecturers. The same volume records that Associated Students conducted the elections for class officers, Who's Who and Homecoming queen, held the October mock election for governor, ran a symposium at which students could question administrators, sponsored the Homecoming dance, and revived the Kentucky Student Association among the state's student governments, with several meetings held at Western.
events.money: 1,175 of Western's 11,000 students voted in the 21 October mock election

src.label: 1972 Talisman, Associated Students sections, pp. 57 and 272-73

events.title: Congress approves its committees for the year
events.body: The Herald reported on 10 September 1971 that the Associated Students had approved its committees for the year. The archive does not hold the article's text, so which committees and their assignments are not established.

events.title: Constitution Revision Committee releases its findings
events.body: Travis Witt reported in the Herald of 21 September 1971 that the Constitution Revision Committee had released its findings. The archive does not hold the article's text, so what the committee found is not established.

events.title: An amendment passes in the autumn balloting
events.body: The Herald reported that an amendment passed easily in the same balloting that elected Hugh Campbell freshman president. The archive does not hold the article's text, so what the amendment changed is not established.

events.title: Associated Students asks a Herald reporter to leave
events.body: Roger Miller reported that the Associated Students had asked a reporter to leave. Congress passed a bill to open its meetings thirteen months later, in March 1973.

events.title: Congress approves the new constitution
events.body: The Herald of 3 March 1972 reported that Congress had approved the new constitution. The archive does not hold the article's text, so the vote count and the meeting's other business are not established.

events.title: Students approve the new constitution
events.body: Roger Miller reported in the Herald of 31 March 1972 that students had given their approval to the new Associated Students constitution. The archive does not hold the article's text, so the vote count, turnout, and the constitution's specific changes are not established from this source.

events.title: A board rules that Kim Weaver can seek ASG office
events.body: John Lucas reported in the Herald of 7 April 1972 that a board had ruled presidential candidate Kim Weaver could seek Associated Student Government office. The same issue carried two further headlines on conflict over the ruling, by Carter Pence and Roger Miller, describing the Rules and Elections Committee as disgusted with the Judicial Council's handling of the matter. The archive does not hold the articles' text, so which board ruled, on what ground, and the sequence of the earlier rulings are not established.

events.title: The Judicial Council declines to act
events.body: Elaine Ayers reported in the Herald of 14 April 1972 that the Judicial Council had declined to act. The archive does not hold the article's text, so the matter before the council is not established.

executive.name: Reginald Glass
executive.note: Glass was vice president of Associated Students in 1971-72 and the yearbook calls him the first black vice president of the body and the first black student to hold any high student leadership position at Western. As vice president he assisted the president, sat on the Academic Council as one of two voting student members, and chaired the activities committee; a caption of him signing a speaker contract appears beside the yearbook's note that Dr. Benjamin Spock was A.S.'s first sponsored speaker, though the volume does not explicitly say the two are the same contract. He was a member of Alpha Phi Alpha, which received its national charter on 31 October 1971, and the Herald reported that November that he was named the campus's outstanding Black Greek. By October 1973 he was ASG's representative from the Graduate College and the Herald reported him asking for better minority representation in student government; he resigned that post in protest on 4 December 1973, the Herald reported, and the 1974 Talisman gives his reason as the harm he said the lack of Black and foreign students on ASG and the Academic Council did to the minorities and the University alike.
profile: Reginald Glass was elected vice president of the Associated Students for 1971-72 under president Linda Jones, becoming, the 1972 Talisman says, the first Black vice president of the body and the first Black student to hold a top student leadership post at Western. As vice president he sat on the Academic Council as one of its two voting student members and chaired the activities committee; a yearbook caption shows him signing a speaker contract, placed beside the note that Dr. Benjamin Spock was A.S.'s first sponsored speaker, though the volume does not state outright that this was Spock's own contract.

Glass was also active in Black campus life outside ASG: he belonged to Alpha Phi Alpha fraternity, chartered nationally at Western on 31 October 1971, and the Herald reported him named the campus's outstanding Black Greek that November.

He remained involved in student government after his year as vice president ended. By the fall of 1973 he sat in the ASG Congress as the representative from the Graduate College, and the Herald reported him pressing for better representation of minority students in student government and on the Academic Council. On 4 December 1973 the Herald reported that he had resigned that seat in protest; the 1974 Talisman records his reasoning as the harm he said the absence of Black and foreign students from ASG and the Academic Council did to the minorities and to the University.

executive.name: Joe Glasser
executive.note: Glasser was treasurer of Associated Students in 1971-72. A Jack Glasser is separately listed as junior class treasurer in the same volume; the yearbook treats them as two names and this archive should not merge them.
profile: Joe Glasser served as treasurer of the Associated Students for 1971-72, one of the four officers under president Linda Jones. The 1972 Talisman lists him alongside vice president Reginald Glass and secretary Nancy Pape in the officer photograph for that year. The same volume separately lists a Jack Glasser as junior class treasurer; the archive treats them as two people rather than merging the names.

executive.name: Nancy Pape
executive.note: Pape was secretary of Associated Students in 1971-72 under Linda Jones. The volume notes the four A.S. officers attended conferences and meetings at national level during the year.
profile: Nancy Pape served as secretary of the Associated Students for 1971-72 under president Linda Jones, one of four officers the 1972 Talisman says represented Western at conferences and meetings at the national level that year.

members.name: Nancy Burdett
members.note: The yearbook's own name index spells the surname 'Burdette.'

members.name: Marshall Florence
members.note: The yearbook's own name index spells the first name 'Marshal' (one L).

senate.note: The two Associated Students Congress group photographs in the 1972 Talisman, pp. 272-273, name thirty-nine members between them. Thirty-eight are recorded here. The thirty-ninth, printed in the caption as Reed Morgan, is held back deliberately: the archive already carries a Reed Morgan at 1968-69, the unresolved plaque name, and the site builds one person page per name, so recording this one would silently merge the two into a single person shown as serving from 1968-69 to 1971-72. The 1972 Talisman puts a Reed Morgan among the Alpha Phi Alpha brothers at that fraternity's charter presentation on 31 October 1971, alongside fellow Congress members George Kendrick and Ed Givens, so a student of that name was certainly active in 1971-72. Whether he is the same man as the plaque's Reed Morgan is not established, and the archive will not assert a career it has not verified.

leaders.name: Edward Jordan, Jr.
leaders.note: Confirmed by direct Herald election coverage: he ran on a platform the paper labeled progressivism, beat Bob Hatfield in the 20 April 1972 election, and the Herald reported the win five days later. Paired on the plaque with Michael Fiorella, the student regent that year.

sources.label: WKU SGA, Former SGA Presidents roster, archived 24 Sep 2001

profile: Jordan ran for the Associated Student Government presidency on a platform the Herald's Roger Miller labeled progressivism, profiled a week before the vote. Congress had separately voted to place his opponent, Bob Hatfield, on the ballot after a dispute over Hatfield's eligibility.

Jordan beat Hatfield in the 20 April 1972 election; the Herald reported his win on 25 April under the headline 'Ed Jordan Wins Top Office,' in the same issue as an editorial by Pence and Carter arguing the new ASG president needed cooperation and support.

Edward Jordan's name entered the Herald's letters columns on November 7, 1972, when he and Charles Boteler urged readers to restore ideals. The digitized index does not label the ASG office Jordan held.
On April 10, 1973, as top ASG offices went on the line in the spring election, a letter praising Ed Jordan ran in the Herald.
Jordan stayed in student politics after his year: in April 1974 he wrote to the Herald judging Steve Henry the most qualified candidate in that spring's races.

leaders.name: Michael Fiorella
leaders.note: Student regent, not president. Sworn in 26 September 1972 alongside gubernatorial appointees Gerald Edds and Chalmer Embry, who Gov. Wendell Ford had named the previous month.
profile: In September 1972 the Herald profiled Michael Fiorella, the Associated Student Government vice president, under the headline that he was anti-apathy.
A week later the Herald reported that Fiorella had won the student seat on the Board of Regents.
Fiorella was sworn in on September 26, 1972, alongside Gerald Edds and Chalmer Embry, the board's two other new members.

events.title: Gov. Wendell Ford names two regents
events.body: Gerald Edds and Chalmer Embry. The same issue reports the best ASG course evaluation yet, students questioning the $5 car registration fee, and filing opening for ASG offices.

events.title: Three new regents sworn in, one of them a student
events.body: Michael Fiorella took the student seat alongside Edds and Embry. The same issue reports 'Slack Time at Associated Student Government Congress', an ASG bankruptcy plan and the open-dorm visitation fight continuing.

events.title: A year of involvement promised
events.body: The Herald opened the year reporting Associated Student Government plans for a year of involvement, in an issue that also covered the regents approving a five dollar vehicle registration fee.

events.title: Course evaluation called the best yet
events.body: The Herald judged ASG's course evaluation the best yet, as filing opened for fall ASG offices.

events.title: Five file for student regent; cheerleader ruling deplored
events.body: Five students filed for the student seat on the Board of Regents. In the same issue, an ASG resolution deplored a cheerleader ruling as the university bowed to Black students' demands after a bitter squabble over squad selection.

events.title: Funds fly as Chicago is booked
events.body: ASG funds flew as the group set a Chicago concert, corrected a tactical error by adding more polls to a campus vote, and made its student activity card available.

events.title: Fiorella wins the regent seat
events.body: Michael Fiorella, the Associated Student Government vice president, won the student seat on the Board of Regents. Days earlier the Herald had profiled him as anti-apathy.

events.title: ASG rejects Downing's position on Black affairs
events.body: The Associated Student Government rejected President Dero Downing's position on an Office of Black Affairs, one of the sharpest confrontations of the fall. A congressman's letter the same day called criticism of ASG unjustified.

events.title: Students as campus cops
events.body: ASG wanted students serving as campus police, the Herald reported, while the editorial page argued more time was needed between elections.

events.title: Top offices on the line
events.body: Top Associated Student Government offices went on the line in the day's election, and a letter writer praised Ed Jordan as the voting opened.

events.title: Ed Jordan's theme is progressivism
events.body: The Herald profiled presidential candidate Ed Jordan ahead of the ASG election, describing his campaign theme as progressivism.

events.title: Jordan and Hatfield face off for the presidency
events.body: Ed Jordan and Bob Hatfield contested the ASG presidency in the day's election, after Congress had voted to place Hatfield on the ballot. The same issue carried both candidates' comments on key election issues.

events.title: Jordan wins the presidency
events.body: The Herald reported Ed Jordan's win under the headline 'Ed Jordan Wins Top Office,' alongside an editorial by Pence and Carter arguing the new ASG president needed cooperation and support to succeed.

events.title: ASG sponsors a book exchange, fights a recycling ordinance
events.body: Associated Student Government sponsored a student book exchange. The same issue reported a city recycling ordinance had left ASG holding the bag on trash collection for its paper-recycling program.

events.title: ASG considers aid to a North Vietnam hospital
events.body: Associated Student Government considered sending aid to a hospital in North Vietnam, the Herald's Carter Pence reported, as the Paris Peace Accords negotiations neared their end.

events.title: Registration week grows into a street dance and two mini-concerts
events.body: ASG expanded its registration week programme in autumn 1972 to include a street dance and two mini-concerts. The Talisman counted this among the activities of the Activities Committee under vice president Mike Fiorella.

events.title: ASG activity card goes on sale
events.body: The Herald announced that the ASG activity card was available. The Talisman described it as a programme begun two years earlier that admitted part-time students and the spouses of students to ASG activities for a nominal charge.

events.title: Chicago plays a free concert
events.body: ASG presented Chicago on 4 October 1972 as a free concert, with pianist Robert Lamm fronting the horn section. The Talisman called it one of the season's hottest entertainment nights and said the band was soon forgotten once Jethro Tull arrived three weeks later.

events.title: Buffalo Bob Smith revives the Howdy Doody show in Van Meter
events.body: ASG brought Buffalo Bob Smith and his revival of the Howdy Doody show to Van Meter Auditorium in October 1972. The Talisman called the two-and-a-half hour programme professional and a huge success, with Smith leading a rendition of 'Clarabell the Clown' and playing Chopin, Mozart and Bach.

events.title: Jethro Tull sells tickets and loses money
events.body: Ian Anderson brought Jethro Tull to Diddle Arena on 26 October 1972. Many in the audience called it the best concert ever staged at Western, but the Talisman recorded that the pay concert was a major financial loss for ASG.
events.money: a major financial loss for ASG, amount not stated

events.title: Pat Paulsen opens the lecture programme at Homecoming
events.body: ASG sponsored the political comedian Pat Paulsen on the evening of 1 November 1972, in Homecoming week, with a lecture titled 'Pat Paulsen Looks at the 70's'. The Talisman recorded that ASG's lecture programme for the year began with him.

events.title: The Beach Boys disappoint on Homecoming Friday
events.body: ASG sponsored the Beach Boys in Diddle Arena on Friday 3 November 1972. Students had come to hear the music of the sixties and heard little of it; the Talisman reported the concert was not well received until the band turned to its golden oldies, and that many went home disappointed.

events.title: ASG Homecoming Dance closes the day
events.body: The ASG Homecoming Dance in the Garrett Conference Center Ballroom concluded the full day of Homecoming activities on 4 November 1972. It followed the game against Middle Tennessee and the reception in Diddle Arena.

events.title: Orphan plays a mini-concert to a poor crowd
events.body: The rock band Orphan played an ASG mini-concert on the Wednesday night of 15 November 1972. Al Cross reviewed it for the Herald under the headline that Orphan gave a bad crowd good music.

events.title: ASG loses money on the fall concerts
events.body: Al Cross reported in the Herald that ASG had lost money on its fall concerts. The Talisman confirmed the loss on fall entertainment without giving a figure, and the shortfall shaped the argument over the head fee that ran into the spring.
events.money: loss on fall concerts, figure not given in the sources consulted

events.title: Four free mini-concerts and the Cellar coffee house
events.body: ASG provided four free mini-concerts over the year, by Voice of Cheese, Tiny Alice, Orphan, and Rolfe Kempf with David McHugh. Weekend performances at the Cellar coffee house in West Hall rounded out the music ASG offered; the Talisman counted seven mini-concerts across the year in all.

events.title: The ASG Newsletter finally appears
events.body: After two years in the planning stages, the ASG Newsletter began publication with the November 1972 issue. It came out monthly and was meant to keep students aware of what was happening on campus.

events.title: ASG takes up the idea of a Free University
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG would consider establishing a Free University. The programme of no-cost, no-credit evening courses in subjects such as knitting, photography and yoga began the following spring under coordinator Glenn Jackson.

events.title: ASG schedules a venereal disease symposium
events.body: ASG scheduled a symposium on venereal disease, run in cooperation with Operation Venus and billed as 'V.D. Day'. The Talisman recorded that it was open to Western students, high school students and the public.

events.title: ASG announces a book exchange
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG would begin a book exchange. Congress had passed a bill to initiate a textbook exchange on campus, and the exchange ran at the start of the spring semester.

events.title: Student discount programme runs a sixth year
events.body: ASG's student discount programme continued for a sixth year, contracting with Bowling Green merchants who gave discounts to students. Plans were made to return to a discount coupon book alongside the discount card to increase use of the service.

events.title: Dance opens the spring season to two-thirds of a ballroom
events.body: ASG opened the spring semester on 2 February 1973 with the rock group Dance in the Garrett Ballroom. The Talisman said the mixture of blues-soul, Latin rock and hard rock made it hard to stay seated, but no more than two-thirds of the seats were filled.

events.title: Few attend the ASG symposiums
events.body: The Herald reported that few students attended the ASG symposiums. The venereal disease symposium had been the flagship of the series.

events.title: Stevie Wonder draws 3,850 and costs ASG up to $5,000
events.body: ASG presented Stevie Wonder with Billy Paul and Whole Oats as the first major concert of the second semester, on Tuesday 13 February 1973. The reviews said Wonder was wondrous, but only 3,850 were on hand and ASG lost between $4,000 and $5,000.

events.title: Buckminster Fuller lectures on 'Humans in the Universe'
events.body: The University Lecture Series and ASG jointly sponsored Buckminster Fuller, who spoke on 'Humans in the Universe' on 27 February 1973. The same joint series brought Steve Atlas of Nader's Raiders, who addressed about forty-five ASG Congress members and other interested people.

events.title: Coretta Scott King and Betty Friedan speak on the joint lecture series
events.body: Coretta Scott King and Betty Friedan were both sponsored by the 1972-73 University Lecture Series and ASG. King lectured on excerpts from her book on men's freedoms and their responsibilities; Friedan, called the mother superior of women's lib, spoke on women's liberation. The Talisman does not date either lecture.

events.title: Free University adds seven classes
events.body: The Herald reported that the Free University planned to add seven new classes. The programme of free evening courses was in its first semester.

events.title: Ron Beck calls a concert a mistake
events.body: Al Cross reported in the Herald that Ron Beck, the assistant dean of student affairs who handled concert booking, called a concert a mistake. Beck's judgment on which acts belonged on campus was the standing constraint on ASG's programme for the rest of the decade.

events.title: Congress votes a referendum on raising the head fee
events.body: ASG Congress voted to hold a student referendum on raising the head fee, a week after a Herald editorial argued the fee needed a boost to insure the quality of ASG entertainment. The regents instead voted an increase in ASG's allotment that August.

events.title: Lester Flatt headlines the Bluegrass Festival
events.body: ASG closed its season on 29 April 1973 with a Bluegrass and Folk Crafts Festival headlined by Lester Flatt and the Nashville Grass, with Mac Wiseman and II Generation. It was the second consecutive year the festival had been held.

events.title: ASG announces a paper recycling project
events.body: The Herald of 6 October 1972 reported that Associated Student Government would launch a paper recycling project. The 1973 Talisman recorded that the project ran: paper was collected in ecology trash cans set at points across campus, collection was later extended to cans and bottles, and the money from the sale of recycled paper went back into the work of the Environmental Committee, which Joe Cheak headed.

events.title: Jimmy Buffett played an ASG mini-concert
events.body: The Herald of 17 April 1973 billed a mini-concert by Jimmy Buffett for that Thursday. The 1973 Talisman records that Buffett came to campus on 19 April in levis and a cowboy shirt carrying two Martin guitars, and counts him among the two major concerts, three mini-concerts and Bluegrass Festival that ASG sponsored that spring semester.

events.title: Congress college elections are partly voided after a ballot discrepancy
events.body: A count of the 1972 Homecoming Queen election showed a difference of 275 between ballots cast and voters recorded. ASG's Rules and Elections Committee called for a re-election of the queen and declared only the Who's Who vote and the Congress elections for three colleges valid. The re-vote was held on the Friday before Homecoming Day and was disrupted for over an hour when a group of Black students blocked the polls; the polls reopened shortly before 10 a.m. after their leaders met ASG officers.

events.title: Congress votes to appeal a Student Affairs decision
events.body: Carter Pence reported that the ASG Congress had voted to appeal a decision of the office of Student Affairs. The archive does not hold the article's text, so the decision appealed and the outcome are not established.

events.title: ASG resubmits a bill of rights
events.body: Carter Pence reported that ASG had resubmitted its bill of rights. John Lyne's 1971 account had described the drafting of a student code of rights as part of the constitutional effort. The archive does not record what became of the resubmitted document.

events.title: Fiorella proposes a $3.50 head fee increase
events.body: Al Cross reported activities vice president Mike Fiorella proposing a $3.50 increase in the head fee to improve the quality of entertainment. Congress voted on 24 April to put the increase to a student referendum, and the Herald reported the vote set for 2 May 1973.

events.title: Congress passes a bill to open its meetings
events.body: Steven Russell reported that ASG had passed a bill to open its meetings, thirteen months after the Associated Students asked a Herald reporter to leave.

events.title: A Congress resolution and petition produce a presidential committee on housing
events.body: After weeks of debate that included an ASG resolution and a committee petition requesting an open visitation policy, President Dero Downing appointed a thirteen-member committee of eight faculty members and five students to study overall university housing policies. The 1973 Talisman does not date the appointment.

executive.name: Charles Boteler
executive.note: Boteler was administrative vice president in 1972-73, the first year the office existed in that form. The volume explains that the revised constitution split the vice presidency in two, one for administrative duties and one for activities, and that Boteler and Mike Fiorella held them respectively. Away from ASG that same year, the 1973 Talisman records Boteler co-leading the campus 'McGovern for President' campaign with Pat Long, serving as an alternate delegate pledged to George McGovern at the Democratic National Convention, and helping lead a McGovern-Shriver teach-in on the Vietnam War with faculty members Jim Wayne Miller and Nick Kafoglis.
profile: Charles Boteler was elected administrative vice president of the newly renamed Associated Student Government for 1972-73, the first year the vice presidency was split in two under a revised constitution; Boteler held the administrative half while Mike Fiorella, later that year's student regent, held the activities half.

Boteler was also prominent in campus electoral politics that year. The 1973 Talisman records him co-leading, with Pat Long, the student effort behind George McGovern's 1972 presidential campaign at Western, running a voter-registration drive and organizing for the Warren County Democratic caucus. He served as an alternate delegate pledged to McGovern at the Democratic National Convention, and helped lead a McGovern-Shriver teach-in on the Vietnam War alongside faculty members Jim Wayne Miller and Nick Kafoglis.

executive.name: Pat Newton
executive.note: Newton was ASG treasurer in 1972-73. The same paragraph sets out the remade Congress: ten representatives at large, two from each academic college, the president and vice president of each class, and the ten Academic Council members and alternates. The same volume's Who's Who feature profiles Newton separately as an accounting and economics major who was a member of the business games team and of Who's Who Among Student Leaders of America, and who served as both president and treasurer of Alpha Delta Pi sorority.
profile: Pat Newton served as treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1972-73, under the constitution that remade the Congress to include ten representatives at large and two from each academic college alongside the class officers and Academic Council delegation.

The 1973 Talisman's Who's Who feature profiles Newton separately from her ASG role: an accounting and economics major, she was a member of the business games team and was named to Who's Who Among Student Leaders of America. She also served as both treasurer and president of Alpha Delta Pi sorority.

src.label: 1973 Talisman, Associated Students, and Who's Who, p. 227

executive.name: Debby Clark
executive.note: Clark was ASG secretary in 1972-73, the year the body took the name Associated Student Government in place of the Office of Associated Students.
profile: Debby Clark served as secretary of the Associated Student Government for 1972-73, the year the body adopted that name in place of the earlier Office of Associated Students, under president Ed Jordan alongside vice presidents Charles Boteler and Mike Fiorella and treasurer Pat Newton.

executive.name: Michael Fiorella
executive.note: The archive records Fiorella only as student regent; the sources say he held both offices. The 1973 Talisman states that under the new constitution two vice presidents were elected, one for administrative duties and one for activities, and that Charles Boteler and Mike Fiorella held them respectively; the Herald of 1 September 1972 calls him vice president for activities (https://digitalcommons.wku.edu/dlsc_ua_records/4871) and the 1974 Talisman says he was elected ASG activities vice-president in his junior year and was also student regent. He headed the Activities Committee, which booked Chicago, Jethro Tull and the Beach Boys, and he proposed raising the student activity fee to $5 a semester from the $1.50 then charged, the quoted words being his verdict on the existing funding. A caption in the same volume says he was chosen as the voting student member of the Board of Regents because ASG president Ed Jordan was disqualified for being an out-of-state student, while the volume's Board of Regents page says he was elected student representative by the student body; both statements come from the 1973 Talisman. Sources print him as Mike Fiorella.
profile: This archive's leader record names Michael Fiorella only as the 1972-73 student regent, but the sources say he held both offices at once. The 1973 Talisman states that the newly revised ASG constitution created two vice presidents, one for administrative duties and one for activities, and that Charles Boteler and Mike Fiorella held them respectively; the Herald of 1 September 1972 likewise calls him vice president for activities, and the 1974 Talisman says he was elected ASG activities vice-president in his junior year and was also student regent.

As activities vice president he headed the Activities Committee, which the 1973 Talisman credits with the greatest number of nationally known groups yet booked at Western, naming Chicago, Jethro Tull and the Beach Boys among five concerts that year. The same volume records him arguing for a higher student activity fee than the $1.50 a semester then charged.

Fiorella went on to the voting student seat on the Board of Regents that year; the 1973 Talisman's own account of how he came to hold it is not fully consistent, crediting his selection in one place to Ed Jordan's disqualification as an out-of-state student and in another to election by the student body. He was sworn in on 26 September 1972.

src.label: 1973 Talisman, Associated Students, pp. 74-75, and Profile, p. 237

officers.name: Don Carter
officers.note: Carter led the ten-member Judicial Council in 1972-73, which heard student appeals on parking tickets, dorm campusing and election violations and served as the deciding court for campus rule violations.
profile: Don Carter chaired the ten-member Judicial Council in 1972-73, the body Associated Student Government used as its final court for appeals of campus rule violations, including parking tickets, dorm-campusing penalties and election disputes. The 1973 Talisman, describing the council's work that year, notes that student rights on campus were also handled through disciplinary boards set up in each residence hall to rule on in-hall cases. The archive has found no further record of Carter's time in office.

officers.name: Pat Long
officers.note: Congress unanimously approved Long, a senior speech major from Franklin, Ohio, as parliamentarian at its first meeting of the 1972-73 year, held 31 August 1972. The 1973 Talisman also names him as one of the two students who headed the Legal Rights Committee, which worked on a bail-bond fund for arrested students and on the appeal of the 'Fly' censorship case.
profile: Congress unanimously elected Pat Long parliamentarian at its first meeting of the 1972-73 year, 31 August 1972; the Herald described him as a senior speech major from Franklin, Ohio. The 1973 Talisman also names him, together with Gary Whitfield, as head of the Legal Rights Committee, which worked on a bail-bond fund for arrested students, on the appeal of the 'Fly' movie-censorship case, and pressed the university over the expulsion of students charged but not convicted of drug violations.

Long had run for ASG president that spring and lost. A 31 March 1972 Herald feature profiled him under the headline "Pat Long: Activism is Associated Student Government," and on election day the paper urged support for Ed Jordan over him, while a student action group declined to endorse Long. Jordan won and served as president for 1972-73, the year Long instead held the parliamentarian post and the Legal Rights co-chairmanship. That same spring, Long and Charles Boteler led a group of Western students into the McGovern-for-president campaign, running a voter-registration drive and taking part in the Warren County Democratic caucus that chose delegates to the party's national convention; the 1973 Talisman later names Long president of Western's Young Democrats club.

Long ran for ASG president again in April 1973, one of four candidates -- with Henry Davis, Mike Fiorella and Steve Yater -- whose platforms the Herald covered that spring. Yater won and served as president for 1973-74. The archive has found no further record of Long's activity in student government after that election.

src.label: Herald 52:3, 1 Sep 1972, 'New appointments win ASG approval'

officers.name: Louis Berman
officers.note: Berman was approved by Congress as sergeant-at-arms at the first meeting of the 1972-73 year, in the same vote that made Pat Long parliamentarian.
profile: Louis Berman was elected freshman-class representative at large in fall 1971, one of five officers chosen at the class's first meeting. The following spring he was elected sophomore class president, a post that under ASG's constitution carried an automatic Congress seat; Congress then approved him as sergeant-at-arms on 31 August 1972, in the same vote that made Pat Long parliamentarian. A Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity brother, the 1973 Talisman's chapter page lists 'ASG Sargeant-at-Arms Louis Berman' among its members' honors that year, and its class-of-1974 section, headlined 'Louis Berman Led Sophomores During a Quiet Year,' names him sophomore class president alongside vice-president Michael Inman. The archive has found no further record of his time in the post.

src.label: Herald 52:3, 1 Sep 1972, 'New appointments win ASG approval'

officers.name: R. G. Meade
officers.note: Congress approved Meade as chairman of the Rules and Elections Committee at its first meeting of 1972-73. Speaking as co-chairman of the committee in the same issue, he said filing was so thin that four colleges had only one candidate each for the Academic Council; the quoted words are his. The 1973 Talisman describes the committee as headed by R.G. Meade and Fred Price, and says it set campaign guidelines and heard election disputes, drawing particular attention during the disputed Homecoming Queen election and re-election that autumn. The Herald prints him as R. G. Meade in one story and Robert Meade in another on the same page.
profile: Congress approved R. G. Meade as chairman of the Rules and Elections Committee at its first meeting of the 1972-73 year, 31 August 1972; in the same issue, speaking as co-chairman, he told the Herald that filing was so thin that four colleges had only one candidate each running for their Academic Council seats. The 1973 Talisman describes the committee, headed by Meade and Fred Price, as the body that set campaign guidelines and heard election disputes, and says it drew particular attention that autumn over a disputed Homecoming Queen election and re-election. The Herald itself is inconsistent on his name, printing him as both R. G. Meade and Robert Meade in stories from the same page; the archive keeps both spellings rather than silently choosing one.

src.label: Herald 52:3, 1 Sep 1972, 'New appointments win ASG approval'

officers.name: Joe Cheak
officers.note: ASG's own newsletter of 3 November 1972 calls Cheak committee chairman and reports that he had submitted a list of proposals to the Physical Plant to obtain containers for a campus recycling project; the January 1973 issue records that the first fortnight of collection brought in over a ton and a half of material, mostly newsprint, and that the project nearly ended when the Alton Box Board Co. could not collect the paper. The 1973 Talisman calls the environmental work ASG's most notable achievement in student services that year. A Joe Cheek is listed in the Herald as one of the ten Rules and Elections Committee members approved the same autumn; the two spellings are not reconciled here.
profile: Joe Cheak chaired ASG's Environmental Committee in 1972-73, which the 1973 Talisman calls the year's most notable achievement in student services: the committee's first year of active involvement in campus ecology. ASG's own newsletter of 3 November 1972 names Cheak committee chairman and reports he had already proposed to the university's Physical Plant that it supply containers for a campus paper-recycling drive; the newsletter's January 1973 issue records that the first two weeks of collection brought in more than a ton and a half of material, mostly newsprint, before the project nearly collapsed when the paper company that had agreed to buy it, the Alton Box Board Co., could not collect it. The Talisman adds that the committee went on to add can and bottle recycling, with proceeds funneled back into expanding the program, and that ASG separately began researching banned toys sold by local merchants toward organizing a Kentucky Student Public Interest Research Group.

Cheak also represented the senior class in the Associated Student Congress that year as its vice president, alongside class president Terry Miller; the 1973 Talisman notes the two felt their main duty was representing the class in Congress, and that beyond sponsoring a Homecoming queen candidate the class held no other activities that year. In April 1973 Cheak wrote to the Herald praising outgoing president Ed Jordan. A Herald story from the same autumn also lists a 'Joe Cheek' among ten members approved to the Rules and Elections Committee; the archive does not reconcile the two spellings.

src.label: ASG Newsletter, Vol. 1 No. 1, 3 Nov 1972 (WKU SGA collection)

officers.name: Gary Whitfield
officers.note: The 1973 Talisman says the Legal Rights Committee was headed by Pat Long and Gary Whitfield, and that it dealt with community legal problems involving students, worked to set up a bail-bond fund for arrested students, and pressed the university over the expulsion of students charged but not convicted of drug violations, the refusal to show X-rated films in the student centre and the appeal of the 'Fly' censorship case. The volume uses the word 'headed'; it does not give either man the title of chairman.
profile: The 1973 Talisman names Gary Whitfield, together with Pat Long, as head of ASG's Legal Rights Committee in 1972-73 -- the yearbook uses the word 'headed' rather than a formal title. The committee worked to set up a bail-bond fund for students who were arrested and pressed the university over three issues: the expulsion of students charged but not convicted of drug violations, the refusal to show X-rated films in the student center, and the appeal of the 'Fly' movie-censorship case. The archive has found no further record of Whitfield's time in office.

members.name: Janice Berkshire
members.seat: representative of the College of Applied Arts to the ASG Congress
members.note: The 1973 Talisman's Kappa Delta chapter page records Berkshire as representing the College of Applied Arts in the ASG Congress.
profile: Berkshire represented the College of Applied Arts in the Associated Student Government Congress during 1972-73, according to the Talisman's page on her sorority, Kappa Delta.

members.name: David Brown
members.note: The 1973 Talisman's Sigma Alpha Epsilon chapter page names Brown the chapter's representative to the Academic Council. The same volume's account of the revised constitution puts the Academic Council members and alternates on the roll of Congress, which is the basis for recording him here. The volume does not say whether he sat as a full member or an alternate, or for which college.
profile: Brown served as his fraternity's representative to the Academic Council in 1972-73, according to the Talisman's page on Sigma Alpha Epsilon. The same volume's account of the revised constitution placed Academic Council members and alternates on the roll of Congress, though it does not say whether Brown sat as a full member or an alternate.

members.name: John Burden
members.note: The 1973 Talisman's section on graduate representation names Burden and Steve Schulman as members of the Academic Council for the graduate college. The same volume puts the Academic Council members and alternates on the roll of Congress, which is the basis for recording him here; it does not distinguish full members from alternates.

src.label: 1973 Talisman, Grad students have ASG representation, pp. 465-466

profile: Burden and fellow graduate student Steve Schulman represented the graduate college on the Academic Council in 1972-73, according to the Talisman's section on graduate-student representation. The same volume's account of the revised constitution placed Academic Council members and alternates on the roll of Congress, though it does not say whether Burden sat as a full member or an alternate.

members.name: Robert Deboe
members.note: The 1973 Talisman's Alpha Phi Alpha chapter page records that Deboe was elected to the Associated Student Government during the year the volume covers.

members.name: Gail Emberton
members.note: The 1973 Talisman records the junior class electing Fred Price president and Emberton vice president for the year; under the revised constitution both seats carried a place on the roll of Congress. Her Who's Who entry in the 1974 Talisman names her Chi Omega's personnel chairman and a President's Scholar, and records her taking part in ASG.

src.label: 1973 Talisman, Classes (Juniors), p. 397; 1974 Talisman, Who's Who

profile: Gail Emberton was elected junior class vice-president for 1972-73, serving under president Fred Price. The 1973 Talisman recorded that the revised Associated Students constitution had cut the class slate to two officers, and that the class's Homecoming float, entered with Debby Clark as its queen candidate, won the Red Towel Award. The class also planned a dinner for its active members.

The 1974 Talisman named her to Who's Who among students, listing her as personnel chairman of Chi Omega, 1972-73 junior class vice-president, first runner-up in the Miss Three Alarm contest, and a President's Scholar.

A Gail Emberton bylined Herald housing and academic-affairs reporting through the same year, from dormitory occupancy in January 1973 to the Housing Committee's proposed policy revisions on 1 May. The archive has not confirmed from any source that the reporter and the class vice-president are the same person, and records the byline without asserting it.

members.name: Laurie Flaim
members.note: The 1973 Talisman names Flaim vice president of the freshman class, with Steve Henry as president, the only two class officers that year. Under the revised constitution the same volume describes, the president and vice president of each class sat on the roll of Congress. Her freshman portrait in that volume prints the name Laurel A. Flaim, a spelling variant not otherwise noted. A Herald report would give the vote; the archive has not read it.

members.name: Merlin Gagle
members.seat: ASG representative from the Graduate College
members.note: The 1973 Talisman's section on graduate representation names Gagle and Juanita Morrow as student government representatives from the graduate college. He was found while checking Morrow's seat and was not on the list this pass began from; the sentence that carries her name carries his.

members.name: Mark Harvey
members.seat: representative at large to the ASG Congress
members.note: The 1973 Talisman's Sigma Nu chapter page records Harvey as a representative-at-large to the Associated Student Government Congress.

members.name: Steve Henry
members.note: The 1973 Talisman's Classes section records the freshman class electing Henry president, with Laurie Flaim as vice president, the only two class officers that year; under the revised constitution both seats carried a place on the roll of Congress. The Sigma Alpha Epsilon chapter page in the same volume calls the freshman class president Pledge Steve Harvey; the Classes section spelling is followed here. A Herald report would give the vote; the archive has not read it.

members.name: Michael Inman
members.note: The 1973 Talisman records the sophomore class electing Louis Berman president and Inman vice president the previous spring. The same volume's account of the constitution puts class presidents and vice presidents in the Congress with a vote, which is the basis for recording him here. A Herald report of the meeting of 31 August 1972 would show what committee work he was given; the archive has not read it.
profile: Michael Inman entered the Associated Students Congress by the class-officer route. The 1973 Talisman records the sophomore class electing Louis Berman president and Inman vice-president the previous spring, and the same volume's account of the revised constitution places class presidents and vice-presidents on the roll of Congress with a vote. The yearbook's account of the class year is thin: a large class that took part in few class projects and put its effort into a single Homecoming queen candidate, Elaine Leftwich. Later volumes give his home as Harrodsburg.

src2.label: 1975 Talisman, senior directory, p. 361

members.name: Terry Miller
members.note: The 1973 Talisman records Miller as senior class president with Joe Cheak as vice president, and says the two took their responsibility to be representing the class in the Associated Students Congress, class activity being nil for the rest of the year. A caption in the same volume says the two represented the senior class in the Congress.
profile: Terry Miller held class office in two consecutive years. The 1972 Talisman lists him as junior class vice-president for 1971-72, one of five class officers headed by president Ed Jordan, who became Associated Students president the following year; that volume says the class structure carried no separate power of its own and left its officers to direct their attention at the A.S. Congress. For 1972-73 Miller was elected senior class president, with Joe Cheak as vice-president.

The 1973 Talisman recorded that the number of class officers had been cut to two that year, and that Miller and Cheak understood their responsibility as representing the class in the Associated Students Congress; the yearbook reported that class activity was otherwise nil, the only class project being to sponsor Lee Davis as a Homecoming queen candidate.

members.seat: ASG representative from the Graduate College
members.note: The 1973 Talisman's section on graduate representation names Morrow and Merlin Gagle as student government representatives from the graduate college. The volume does not say which kind of seat she held; a Herald report of the vote of 19 September 1972 would settle it and has not been read.

members.name: Fred Price
members.seat: junior class president; co-head, Rules and Elections Committee
members.note: The 1973 Talisman records Price as junior class president, with Gail Emberton as vice president, and names him and R. G. Meade as heads of the Rules and Elections Committee. Under the revised constitution the class presidency carried a place on the roll of Congress. A Herald report of the meeting of 31 August 1972 would show how the committee was constituted; the archive has not read it.

profile: Fred Price was elected junior class president for 1972-73 with Gail Emberton as vice-president. The 1973 Talisman noted that under the revised Associated Students constitution only the top two class officers were retained, and that class presidents and vice-presidents had previously been allowed to vote in Congress. The yearbook recorded the class's Homecoming float as winner of the Red Towel Award, with Debby Clark as its queen candidate.

The same yearbook recorded the Rules and Elections Committee, which handles campus elections and hears election disputes, as headed by R. G. Meade and Fred Price. That committee was tested in the first week of November 1972, when a voting discrepancy forced a special election for Homecoming queen; the Herald of 4 November 1972 carried the story alongside an item headlined that Fred Price said the committee would investigate the election.

Price stood for Associated Student Government administrative vice president in the spring of 1973. The Herald of 6 April 1973 printed the platforms of the two hopefuls for the office, Glenn Jackson and Fred Price. Jackson took the post for 1973-74. The 1973 Talisman pictures Price in the Pi Kappa Phi colony, and the 1974 volume records the chapter receiving its national charter with Price still a member.

members.note: The 1973 Talisman's section on graduate representation names Schulman and John Burden as members of the Academic Council for the graduate college. members.name: Carl Stolzfus
members.seat: Academic Council representative, College of Education
members.note: The 1973 Talisman's Sigma Phi Epsilon chapter page records him as a member of Associated Students Government, the student member of the Academic Council from the College of Education, and a member of the college's curriculum committee and the university academic complaint committee. The chapter page spells the surname Stoltzfus. A Herald report would give the vote he polled on 19 September 1972; the archive has not read it.
profile: The 1973 Talisman recorded Carl Stoltzfus as a member of the Associated Students Government, the student member of the Academic Council from the College of Education, and a member of both the College of Education Curriculum Committee and the University Academic Complaint Committee. He and fellow Sigma Phi Epsilon member Mike Brandenberg represented their fraternity at the National Leadership Methods Convention. The 1974 volume gives his home as Cochranville, Pennsylvania, and his major as elementary education.

The Herald of 13 April 1973, the issue that carried the Associated Student Government election returns and a report on the installation of officers at the Congress party, printed a letter under his name headlined as thanking his supporters. The archive has not read the letter and cannot say whether he had stood, or for what office.

For 1973-74 he was elected senior class president, with Hamp Moore as vice-president; the 1974 Talisman recorded the pair supervising the class's Homecoming activities and its Gone with the Wind float. That yearbook also listed him as chairman of the Associated Student Government's Rules and Elections Committee, public relations chairman of the Student National Education Association, Talisman Greek editor and a member of Who's Who.

The archive holds his surname in two spellings. Every appearance in the 1973 and 1974 Talisman — the fraternity pages, the Who's Who entry, the senior class pages and both name indexes — gives Stoltzfus, as does the Herald's index of his own 4 December 1973 letter. The single Stolzfus is the Herald's index of his letter of 13 April 1973, which is the spelling the 1972-73 Congress record was built on. The difference is flagged, not resolved.
