leaders.name: Christy Vogt
leaders.note: The plaque reads "Christy Mollozzi". Every contemporaneous source calls her Christy Vogt: she bylined Herald pieces as Vogt through 1976-77, the paper covered her as ASG president under that name, and SGA's own roster of former presidents, archived in September 2001, lists "Christy Vogt, Louisville, 1976-77" and stars her as a student regent. This site follows the sources. Vogt was administrative vice president in 1975-76 before winning the presidency. As with Coates and Lich, and Seay and Taylor, the plaque's later surname is most likely a married name, but no source found states the connection. The Herald's 9 April 1976 headline "Christy Vogt Wins Election" and her own "Winner Says Thanks" the same issue confirm the 1976-77 ASG presidency was won under the name Christy Vogt; her byline runs through the term (campaign endorsement 26 Mar 1976, "Urges Involvement" 12 Apr 1977, the closing letter to Congress 26 Apr 1977). The plaque records her as Christy Mollozzi. WKU's own archive ties the two names together in multiple places written by the university itself, not by this project: a WKU Archives research notecard indexed as "Mollozzi, Christy Vogt," and Christy Mollozzi appearing in the President's Office finding aids for the Meredith and Ransdell administrations in connection with Marketing & Promotions, meaning she had a further career on the WKU staff. "Christy Vogt Mollozzi" follows the ordinary American convention of a married name with the maiden name kept as a middle name. No single source states outright "formerly Christy Vogt," so this is an inference from a consistent name pattern repeated across independent WKU records over three decades, not a documented fact - flagged here rather than asserted as certain.

sources.label: UA37/30/2 WKU Research Notecards-Sources ("Mollozzi, Christy Vogt")
WKU SGA, Former SGA Presidents roster, archived 24 Sep 2001

profile: Christy Vogt entered the spring 1976 Associated Student Government campaign with an endorsement from Herald columnist John Butchko, in an issue whose front section also covered the start of impeachment hearings against congress member Gerard Faulk and an editorial warning the university's new Faculty Senate away from ASG's own troubles.

Vogt and Bruce Smith survived the 2 April primary as the Herald reported 527 ballots cast, then Vogt won the presidency outright, the paper reporting the result on 9 April 1976 under the headline "Christy Vogt Wins Election," with her own note of thanks to voters in the same issue - the same week Faulk was acquitted.

In office for 1976-77, Vogt's congress created a constitutional revision committee within its first month (Bill 2, 7 September 1976) and kept revision on its agenda all year. It asked the university for a minimum wage policy for student employees (Resolution, 26 October 1976), recommended preregistration for all students, and opposed a proposed tuition increase (Bill 9, 8 March 1977) while creating a Complaint Committee to field student grievances the same meeting. A resolution on discrimination failed in February 1977 with fourteen members abstaining. The fall Seals and Crofts concert lost the organization $3,800, a recurring sore point ASG had wrestled with under Vogt's predecessors as well.

Vogt wrote her own case for the office in the Herald - "Urges Involvement," 12 April 1977, days before Bob Moore won the presidency to succeed her by a 26-vote margin. She closed her term on 26 April 1977 with a letter to Congress thanking its members and recommending four items to the administration: constitutional revision, extended hours for student buildings, open visitation, and advance registration - the same four causes her congress had pushed all year.

WKU's own archive later indexes her, alongside her maiden name, as Christy Vogt Mollozzi, and separately as Christy Mollozzi in President's Office records tied to Marketing & Promotions - evidence, though not a documented statement, that she went on to a career on the university's own staff.

events.title: Bob Moore elected ASG president by 26 votes
events.body: One of the narrowest margins in the record. The same issue carries the outgoing president congratulating voters, the faculty asking for a say in hiring, and Western fighting a beer licence for a local pizzeria.

events.title: Four candidates open the race to succeed Vogt
events.body: The Herald previewed a crowded ASG election: Tom Blair, Kirt Grubbs, Mark McChesney and Bob Moore all sought the presidency, with voting set for a Tuesday primary. Three candidates ran for the administrative vice presidency and four for the activities post in the same election.

events.title: ASG creates constitutional revision committee
events.body: The Associated Student Government congress passed Bill 2, creating a committee charged with revising the organization's constitution. Constitutional revision remained on the ASG agenda for the rest of the school year and appeared again among proposed amendments and a spring referendum bill.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Bill 2 - Constitutional Revision Committee, 7 Sep 1976

events.title: ASG asks WKU for a student minimum wage
events.body: The congress adopted Resolution 13, proposing that Western institute a minimum wage policy for all student employees. It was part of a heavy fall docket that also included resolutions on parking, laundry services, non-smoking areas and residence hall change machines.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Resolution 13 - Minimum Wage, 26 Oct 1976

events.title: Seals and Crofts concert loses ASG $3,800
events.body: The Herald reported that the Seals and Crofts concert set the Associated Student Government back $3,800. Concert finances would remain a recurring sore point for ASG through the rest of the decade.

events.title: ASG recommends preregistration for all students
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG would recommend preregistration for all students. Advance registration was one of the four items president Christy Vogt later carried into her end-of-year recommendations to the administration.

events.title: Discrimination resolution fails as 14 abstain
events.body: Fourteen members abstained as the Associated Student Government rejected a resolution on discrimination, the Herald reported. The same issue noted that filing for ASG posts would begin the following Monday.

events.title: Bill calls for ASG to evaluate itself
events.body: Bill 6 proposed that the Associated Student Government conduct a self-evaluation "for the purposes of transparency and improvement."

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Bill 6 - ASG Evaluation, 15 Feb 1977

events.title: ASG passes bill opposing tuition increase
events.body: The congress approved Bill 9, formally opposing a proposed tuition increase. The same March meeting produced Bill 8, which created a Complaint Committee to handle student grievances.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Bill 9 - Opposition to Tuition Increase, 8 Mar 1977

events.title: Vogt closes the congress with four recommendations
events.body: President Christy Vogt sent a letter closing the congress and thanking ASG members for their work. She left four items to recommend to the administration: constitutional revision, extended hours for student buildings, open visitation and advanced registration.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Christy Vogt Letter, 26 Apr 1977

events.title: Vogt urges involvement as her term closes
events.body: With her term nearly over, president Christy Vogt wrote "Urges Involvement" for the Herald, days before Bob Moore's election to succeed her.

events.title: ASG and the Center Board publish the 1976-77 events schedule
events.body: The summer Herald carried the University Center Board and ASG schedule of events for 1976-77. By late August the Herald was reporting two lectures and two concerts on ASG's entertainment slate and that ASG was seeking an appearance by Chicago.

events.title: Lori Wolfson opens the mini-concert series
events.body: ASG continued its mini-concert series with the acoustic guitarist Lori Wolfson in Van Meter Auditorium on 10 September 1976. The second, on 22 September, was Jerico Harp, whose Jim Thomas and Tom Schmidt mixed their own material with songs including Dan Fogelberg's 'Wysteria'.

events.title: 400 books sold in the ASG and Veterans on Campus co-op
events.body: The Herald reported that 400 books had been sold in the book co-op ASG ran with Veterans on Campus. The exchange had been advertised in the first issue of the year.

events.title: Students petition for their Maranatha concert money back
events.body: Students petitioned ASG for the return of a concert payment connected with the Maranatha Christian Center. ASG voted to refund the Maranatha money on 1 October, and by 8 October the Herald reported the Judicial Council had dropped the ASG-Maranatha case.

events.title: Bob Woodward cancels and comes six months late
events.body: Carl Bernstein was booked to open the lecture season but contracted pneumonia, and his partner Bob Woodward was announced as a substitute before cancelling his Western and University of Kentucky dates for work. Promoters paid the advertising costs for the cancelled lecture, but someone in the ASG office drew a bull's-eye on Woodward's publicity poster; he finally appeared in early April 1977.

events.title: Chicago grosses $53,092 and becomes Western's most successful concert
events.body: Chicago appeared at Diddle Arena on 15 October 1976, drew 10,450 people and grossed $53,092. The 1977 Talisman called it Western's most financially successful concert. The show cost $25,000 and was promoted by Reggae Ltd of St Louis with ASG, the first privately promoted concert at Western; about 5,000 advance tickets were sold, another record, and Ron Beck called it one of the best the university had ever had.

events.title: Seals and Crofts play Homecoming and lose $3,800
events.body: Jim Seals and Dash Crofts returned to Western for the Homecoming concert on Saturday 6 November 1976, with the Cate Brothers opening. About 5,200 attended and the concert lost roughly $3,800; Ron Beck blamed the Saturday date, saying everyone was worn out from the rest of Homecoming day. Afterwards the pair held a fireside chat with about 80 students about their Baha'i faith.

events.title: ASG Homecoming dance with the Back Stabbers and Those Perfections
events.body: For those who wanted livelier Homecoming entertainment, ASG sponsored a dance in the Garrett Conference Center Ballroom featuring the Back Stabbers and Those Perfections. It ran the same weekend as the Seals and Crofts concert.

events.title: Barry Manilow plays free to 7,000 and cuts his set short
events.body: Barry Manilow gave the only free major concert of the semester on Monday 15 November 1976 before 7,000 people. The show cost $23,000, with ticket sales subtracting $10,100 from that; a heckler on the first row put Manilow in a bad mood, so he dropped his commercial set and cut the show by fifteen minutes.
events.money: cost $23,000, less $10,100 in ticket sales; attendance 7,000

events.title: Clive Barnes, John Sears and Vincent Bugliosi on the lecture series
events.body: The lecture season carried Clive Barnes of the New York Times in early November on 'The Plight of the Theatre Today', John Sears, Nixon's 1968 campaign manager and later Reagan's, in late November, and Vincent Bugliosi, the Manson prosecutor and author of 'Helter Skelter', in early December. Members of the ASG lecture committee, David Carwell, Ricky Sheppard and Mike Seiler, hosted the visiting speakers.

events.title: David Frye fills Van Meter with impersonations of Nixon
events.body: The comedian David Frye kept a capacity crowd in Van Meter Hall laughing in mid-September 1976 with impersonations of political figures and film stars, Richard Nixon foremost among them. In January the comedian Robert Klein warmed about 700 people in the Garrett Conference Center ballroom in arctic weather.

events.title: ASG considers cutting off the Volunteer Bureau
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG might discontinue funding for the Student Volunteer Bureau. A week later an editorial argued the bureau should have ASG's support; ASG kept funding it for another year before stopping in May 1978.

events.title: Book exchange sells more than 1,100 books
events.body: The Herald reported that the book exchange had sold more than 1,100 books. It was the strongest showing yet for the co-op ASG ran with Veterans on Campus.

events.title: Ethos returns for a Valentine's Day mini-concert
events.body: Ethos appeared on Valentine's Day 1977 in ASG's mini-concert series. The band had first played Western as an ASG mini-concert in October 1973.

events.title: Rufus and Wild Cherry draw 6,500 to a loud spring show
events.body: Rufus and Wild Cherry headlined the first major spring concert on 23 March 1977, opened by Fresh, whom Ron Beck signed for $500 because they were a favourite of Wild Cherry. About 6,500 attended, roughly 4,000 of them students, and Chaka Khan sang on her birthday; Beck said students told him the concert was too loud and that Rufus did not perform to their expectations.
events.money: attendance about 6,500; opening act Fresh cost $500

events.title: Student discount card covers 29 merchants
events.body: The Herald reported that the student discount card offered reductions from 29 merchants. The same issue carried Rick Kelley's review of a year in which Chicago and Barry Manilow headlined the concerts and a prosecutor and a reporter were among the speakers.

events.title: Jimmy Buffett and the Coral Reefer Band closed the concert year
events.body: The Herald announced on 25 March 1977 that a Jimmy Buffett concert was set for 27 April. The 1977 Talisman records that Buffett and the Coral Reefer Band played Diddle Arena that night, drawing three encores after a ninety-minute set from a small crowd, with highlights from 'Changes in Latitudes, Changes in Attitudes' and tunes from 'Livin' and Dyin' in 3/4 Time', 'A-1-A' and 'Havana Daydreamin''. The concert lost money, and the yearbook counts Buffett among the acts brought to Western in 1976-77 by the ASG concert programme run by activities vice president Rick Kelley.

src.label: 1977 Talisman, Concerts; announced in College Heights Herald 52:47, 25 Mar 1977

events.title: Bill 11 sends the constitutional revision to a referendum
events.body: Congress had created a Constitutional Revision Committee by Bill 2 on 7 September 1976. On 5 April 1977 it passed Bill 11, to hold a referendum on the proposed constitutional revisions.

src.label: SGA Bill 11 - Forward Constitutional Revision, 5 Apr 1977

executive.name: Tom Blair
executive.note: Elected on 6 and 7 April 1976 by 570 votes to John David Evans's 552, one of the closest races that spring. The 1977 Talisman lists him with the year's other officers as already having ASG experience. At the 6 April 1976 congress meeting, before the vote on Gerard Faulk, he moved to drop the impeachment proceedings without a vote on removal, and withdrew the motion at the urging of several congressmen. He ran for president the following April and lost to Bob Moore, 562 to 536.
profile: Tom Blair was elected administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government on 6 and 7 April 1976, beating John David Evans by 570 votes to 552 in one of the closest races that spring; the 1977 Talisman lists him among the year's officers as already having ASG experience. About a year earlier, the Herald's 1 April 1975 issue had reported that Blair wanted a president's council formed, with no indication in the sources checked that he then held ASG office himself.

At the 6 April 1976 Congress meeting, before a vote on the impeachment of congressman Gerard Faulk, Blair moved to drop the proceedings without a vote on removal, then withdrew the motion at the urging of several other congressmen. The Herald's 13 April 1976 issue separately reported that Blair withdrew charges he had brought against President Steve Henry; the archive records those charges, one of the two cases behind Faulk's impeachment, as an allegation that Henry had obstructed an advisory intramurals committee.
Blair ran for the ASG presidency himself the following April and lost to Bob Moore, 562 votes to 536.

executive.name: David Payne
executive.note: The 1977 Talisman records Payne and Rick Kelley as the two officers beginning second terms in 1976-77. Note for the editor: years.json separately carries a David Payne who succeeded Marcel Bush as ASG president in January 1982, filed under 1981-82 (not 1982-83) with year_confidence "corrected" - Board of Regents minutes of 30 January 1982 already confirm that identification, so he is not simply an unresolved name. Whether the 1981-82 president is the same person as this 1970s ASG treasurer is not established by any source found so far, and this archive should not merge them without one that links them.
profile: David Payne returned as treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1976-77, one of two officers, along with activities vice president Rick Kelley, beginning a second consecutive term that year, the 1977 Talisman recorded.

Note for the editor: years.json separately carries a David Payne who succeeded Marcel Bush as ASG president in January 1982, filed under 1981-82 (not 1982-83) with year_confidence "corrected" - Board of Regents minutes of 30 January 1982 already confirm that identification, so he is not simply an unresolved name. Whether the 1981-82 president is the same person as this 1970s ASG treasurer is not established by any source found so far, and this archive should not merge them without one that links them.

executive.name: Pam Keown
executive.note: Elected on 6 and 7 April 1976 with 731 votes to Sally Chenault's 501. The 1977 Talisman lists her among the officers who came into the year with ASG experience.
profile: Pam Keown was elected secretary of the Associated Student Government on 6 and 7 April 1976, beating Sally Chenault by 731 votes to 501. The 1977 Talisman lists her among the year's officers who came into the term with prior ASG experience, though the archive has not established what that earlier role was.

executive.name: Rick Kelley
executive.note: Re-elected on 6 and 7 April 1976 over Robert Tackett, 705 to 496, for a second term running the concert programme. He presided over the 6 April 1976 congress meeting in the absence of president Steve Henry. The 1977 Talisman describes him taking acts to the concert selection committee for approval and working with assistant dean of student affairs Ron Beck; the Seals and Crofts homecoming concert lost about $3,800. His surname is printed both Kelley and Kelly in these volumes and the spelling is not settled.
profile: Rick Kelley was re-elected activities vice president of the Associated Student Government on 6 and 7 April 1976, beating Robert Tackett 705 votes to 496 for a second term running Western's concert program. He presided over the 6 April 1976 Congress meeting in President Steve Henry's absence.

A 1977 Talisman feature on his two years in the office, published as his term ended, described how Kelley worked with the concert selection committee and assistant dean of student affairs Ron Beck to book acts. When an agent representing Chicago called offering the band for a $25,000 show, Kelley discussed it with Beck, found a private promoter willing to cover the cost, then took the arrangement to the concert committee for approval; the show, a first for Western with a privately promoted act, set an advance-ticket sales record; Kelley said the show sold out of advance tickets and grossed over $50,000, while the Talisman's own concert report noted that the concert itself was not a sellout despite the record advance sales. The Seals and Crofts homecoming concert that same year drew about 5,200 people but lost roughly $3,800, which assistant dean of student affairs Ron Beck attributed to a Saturday date competing with other homecoming events. Kelley told the yearbook that Beck bore the brunt of student criticism over concert choices, and that students who complained about a show rarely wrote in when one succeeded. His surname is printed both Kelley and Kelly across these volumes; the spelling is not settled.

officers.name: Gerard Faulk
officers.note: Faulk was acquitted of incompetence charges by Congress on 6 April 1976 and the Herald reported that he would conclude a two-year term in office during the 1976-77 ASG session. No later report of a successor was found in this archive.
profile: Faulk continued to chair the Judicial Council into 1976-77, the second year of the two-year term the Herald reported he held, having been acquitted that April of an impeachment brought over his handling of two cases before the council. No later report of a successor has been found in this archive.

officers.name: Mike Pearson
officers.note: Pearson ran the April 1977 general election and told the Herald that no one had been turned away from the polls, against complaints about long voting lines.
profile: Mike Pearson chaired ASG's Rules and Elections Committee in 1976-77 and ran the general election that April. Against complaints about long lines at the polls, he told the Herald that no one had been turned away from voting. The archive has found no further record of his time in office.

members.name: George Carlson
members.note: Nominated, though not elected, as a State Student Government Convention delegate (22 Feb 1977 minutes), which name the nominee George Carlson. A Georgiana Carlson is recorded in years.json under 1977-78 as the losing candidate for ASG treasurer, 437 votes to Gary Reed's 554 (Herald 52:53, 15 Apr 1977), and the 1977 Talisman names a Georgiana Carlson organizing the Rules and Elections committee; whether the minutes' George Carlson is that person, or another, is not established. Congress membership itself is not confirmed by the minutes.
profile: Carlson was nominated as a delegate to the Associated Student Government's State Student Government Convention delegation at Congress's 22 February 1977 meeting; the minutes name him as the nominee, but the two convention-delegate seats that meeting elected went to Bill Cortus and Kevin Kinnie, so Carlson was not elected, and his Congress membership itself is not established by that source. A Georgiana Carlson appears elsewhere in this record as the losing candidate for ASG treasurer in the April 1977 election and as an organizer of that year's Rules and Elections committee; whether she and this nominee were the same person, or two members of the same family, has not been established.

members.name: Bill Cortus
members.note: Gave a Housing Committee report to Congress and was elected one of two delegates to the State Student Government Convention at the same 22 February 1977 meeting; Congress membership itself is not conclusively established by the minutes. Already recorded in years.json under 1977-78 as the losing candidate for Activities Vice President, 510 votes to Brent Shockley's 532 (Herald 52:53, 15 Apr 1977) - the same person, a year earlier.
profile: Cortus gave a Housing Committee report to Congress and was elected one of two delegates to the State Student Government Convention at the 22 February 1977 meeting, though his Congress membership is not conclusively established by that source. The following spring he ran for Activities Vice President and lost to Brent Shockley, 532 votes to 510, in the April 1977 election.

members.name: John Evans
members.note: Reported the year's progress of the Student Affairs Committee to Congress and moved to waive the rules and vote immediately on Bill No. 12, seconded by Tim Leigh; the bill passed 31-0-1 (19 Apr 1977 minutes). The 1977 Talisman separately records a John Evans elected to the student affairs committee before the 1976 summer recess. Not established as the same John David Evans who lost the 1976 Activities Vice President race to Tom Blair, per a separate years.json record - no source found linking the two.
profile: Evans was named on the Associated Student Government's printed Congress attendance roll effective 6 April 1976. The following year, serving on the Student Affairs Committee, he reported the committee's progress to Congress and moved to waive the rules and vote immediately on Bill No. 12, a motion seconded by Tim Leigh that passed 31 to 0 with one abstention at the 19 April 1977 meeting. The 1977 Talisman separately records a John Evans elected to the student affairs committee before the 1976 summer recess. He is not established as the same John David Evans who lost the 1976 election for Activities Vice President to Tom Blair; no source links the two.

members.name: Kevin Kinnie
members.note: Nominated and elected one of two delegates to the State Student Government Convention (22 Feb 1977 minutes); seconded Lynn Moss's motion to bring Bill No. 12 to the floor, which passed 31-0-1 (19 Apr 1977 minutes).
profile: Kinnie served in the Associated Student Government Congress across at least three years. In 1976-77 he was nominated and elected one of two delegates to the State Student Government Convention, and seconded Lynn Moss's motion to bring Bill No. 12 to the floor for an immediate vote, which passed 31 to 0 with one abstention at the 19 April 1977 meeting. The 1978 Talisman indexed him, as a Congress representative, under the fuller name Kevin Robert Kinne. By 1980-81 he chaired both the Academic Affairs and the Student Opinion Poll committees, and at Congress's 11 November 1980 meeting moved that the secretary send Congress's official congratulations to Coach Feix and the football team for winning the 1980 Ohio Valley Conference championship; the motion passed.

members.name: Tim Leigh
members.note: Brought Resolution No. 24 to the floor, seconded by Gene Saunders, which passed 34-0-1, and seconded John Evans's motion to waive the rules and vote immediately on Bill No. 12 (19 Apr 1977 minutes). Also reported for the Academic Affairs Committee (22 Feb and 19 Apr 1977 minutes). The 1977 Talisman separately records him taking responsibility for the academic affairs committee.
profile: Leigh was named on the Associated Student Government's printed Congress attendance roll effective 6 April 1976. The following year, serving on the Academic Affairs Committee, he reported for the committee at Congress's 22 February and 19 April 1977 meetings, brought Resolution No. 24 to the floor (seconded by Gene Saunders, passed 34 to 0 with one abstention), and seconded John Evans's motion to waive the rules and vote immediately on Bill No. 12, which also passed. The 1977 Talisman separately records him taking responsibility for the academic affairs committee.

members.name: Bob Moore
members.seat: Congress member; Rules and Elections Committee
members.note: Submitted and read the 1977 campaign regulations, which passed with no opposition (22 Feb 1977 minutes); also nominated, though not elected, as a delegate to the State Student Government Convention at the same meeting. The 1977 Talisman separately names him organizing the Rules and Elections committee. He won the ASG presidency the following April, 562 votes to Tom Blair's 536, and is already recorded in years.json as 1977-78 president Robert Moore (see name-aliases.json, Bob Moore = Robert Moore).

members.name: Lynn Moss
members.note: Moved to bring Bill No. 12 to the floor, seconded by Kevin Kinnie; the bill passed 31-0-1 (19 Apr 1977 minutes).
profile: Moss moved to bring Bill No. 12 to the floor for an immediate vote, a motion seconded by Kevin Kinnie; the bill passed 31 to 0 with one abstention at Congress's 19 April 1977 meeting.

members.name: Gene Saunders
members.note: Presented the guidelines for SGAK (Student Government Association of Kentucky) committee members, which passed with no opposition, and seconded Tim Leigh's Resolution No. 24, which passed 34-0-1 (19 Apr 1977 minutes). Already recorded in years.json under 1977-78 as chairman of the ASG Rules and Elections Committee - the same person, a year earlier as a Congress member.

leaders.name: Robert Moore
leaders.note: Elected ASG president by a 26-vote margin, reported 15 April 1977. Herald bylines call him 'Bob Moore.'

sources.label: WKU SGA, Former SGA Presidents roster, archived 24 Sep 2001

profile: Moore was one of four candidates - with Tom Blair, Kirt Grubbs and Mark McChesney - who opened the 1977 Associated Student Government presidential race on April 1. Moore and Blair survived the primary into the general election; McChesney did not, and by April 12 his letter backing Moore ran in the Herald alongside endorsements for the rest of the ticket, as outgoing president Christy Vogt urged students to get involved. The Herald's April 8 issue had set up the contest alongside the treasurer's race between George Carlson and rivals.

Moore won on April 15, 1977, by 26 votes over Blair - one of the narrowest presidential margins in the record - in an issue that also carried the faculty asking for a say in hiring and Western fighting a beer licence for a local pizzeria.

That October, as president, Moore publicly questioned how freshman candidates in that fall's class elections were spending their campaign money. The comment drew enough pushback that the Herald ran an editorial the same week headlined 'Bob Moore's Comment Isn't Good Politics.'

The archive does not yet show what Moore's administration did over the winter and into the spring beyond the ordinary business of readying his succession - see the 1978 election events below. By September 1978, after his term had ended, the Herald reported that Moore had been found ineligible for another Associated Student Government job; the archive does not yet hold the article's account of why.

events.title: Spending limits set for the coming ASG election
events.body: The Associated Student Government set spending limits for candidates ahead of the spring election that would choose Moore's successor.

events.title: Thornton and Johnson contest the presidency; four offices go uncontested
events.body: Steve Thornton and Ed Johnson faced off for the Associated Student Government presidency, Thornton campaigning on his experience, while four other offices had no opponent on the ballot.

events.title: Johnson contests his loss to Thornton
events.body: Ed Johnson, having lost the presidential race, contested the Associated Student Government election result.

events.title: ASG awaits approval of constitution changes
events.body: The Herald reported that the Associated Student Government was awaiting approval of changes to its constitution as the fall term opened. The story ran alongside a look at how ASG's concert booking process actually worked.

events.title: David Bass named ASG vice president
events.body: The Associated Student Government named David Bass its new vice president. The same issue carried Moore's letter disputing the Herald's editorial on candidate spending.

events.title: ASG and Interhall Council back coed dorm, end of door-ajar rule
events.body: ASG and the Interhall Council backed a coed dorm and abolition of the door-ajar visitation rule. The vote followed weeks in which the two bodies weighed a dorm petition and the Herald urged ASG to represent students in the dorm protest.

events.title: ASG signs Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick
events.body: ASG signed Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick for spring concerts. Ticket sales proved weak, and by late February the Herald was reporting on the organization's concert losses.

events.title: Concert losses will not stop a free concert
events.body: The Herald reported that losses would not halt an ASG free concert, and that ASG had thrown in towels as a bonus for performers. An editorial declared that the cry for better concerts had finally been heard.

events.title: ASG elections held with four offices uncontested
events.body: Students voted in the Associated Student Government elections with four offices uncontested. Candidate Steve Thornton told the Herald his experience was an important factor in the race.

events.title: ASG books its first show of the year
events.body: The Herald reported in the first issue of the year that ASG had booked its first show. The same freshman issue advertised a used book exchange scheduled in West Hall.

events.title: Waylon Jennings plays after a cocaine arrest scare
events.body: Waylon Jennings and Jessi Colter opened the concert year on 9 September 1977 before about 5,000 people. Jennings and his secretary had been arrested in Nashville on a charge of conspiring to possess cocaine and some feared the show would be cancelled, but he was permitted to keep the date; Colter opened with a thirty-minute set before the band Waylon took over.

events.title: ASG proposes a campus shuttle bus
events.body: An ASG proposal said a shuttle bus was needed to relieve crowded parking lots. The Herald had editorialised a month earlier that a shuttle bus was the best answer to the parking problem.

events.title: Charlie Daniels rescues Homecoming after the Atlanta Rhythm Section cancels
events.body: The Atlanta Rhythm Section cancelled its Homecoming concert, and the Charlie Daniels Band came to Western's rescue on Homecoming eve, Thursday 27 October 1977. Daniels was promoting 'Midnight Wind' and played 'Long-Haired Country Boy', 'The South's Gonna Do It Again' and 'Orange Blossom Special'; ARS rescheduled for February.

events.title: Celebrity Ball plays the ASG Homecoming dance
events.body: Celebrity Ball, a rock group from Atlanta, entertained at an ASG-sponsored dance in the Garrett Conference Ballroom on Homecoming night, after the 20-20 tie with Morehead before an estimated 19,750 fans. It was the fiftieth Homecoming since Henry Hardin Cherry conceived the tradition in 1927.

events.title: Dave Mason and Kenny Loggins lose $13,200
events.body: Only 2,916 came to see Dave Mason and Kenny Loggins in Diddle Arena on 8 November 1977, a concert that cost the university about $31,200. The Herald reported a loss of $13,200; both men were riding new gold albums, Mason took one encore and Loggins three, and the shortfall nearly eliminated the free spring concert.

events.title: The book swap is called off for the spring
events.body: The Herald reported that the book swap was off for the spring semester. The same issue carried ASG's plans for its spring activities and a bill to support a state landlord-tenant measure.

events.title: Few tickets sold for the Atlanta Rhythm Section
events.body: The Herald reported that few tickets had been sold for the ASG concert by the Atlanta Rhythm Section. The warning proved accurate a week later.

events.title: Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick lose $12,000 on Valentine's Day
events.body: The Atlanta Rhythm Section finally appeared on 14 February 1978, bringing fellow Atlantans Brick, who opened with 'Dazz' and 'Dusic'. Most of the audience left before ARS took the stage; only 2,346 tickets were sold and the university lost about $12,000. United Black Students had announced in January that it would help arrange for Brick and LTD to appear, but LTD did not.

events.title: Average White Band signed for the free concert
events.body: The Herald reported that groups had been signed for the free ASG concert, with the Average White Band on the bill. ASG had said in February that its losses would not halt the free concert.

events.title: Average White Band and the Ramsey Lewis Trio close the year free, and draw 3,300
events.body: The free spring concert on 18 April 1978 put the Average White Band and the Ramsey Lewis Trio in Diddle Arena and drew about 3,300, ASG's last show of the year. The Scottish group charged $10,000 and the talent fee for the Ramsey Lewis Trio was $5,000; the Herald's reviewer wrote that the band made a concerted effort but the fans were few.
events.money: AWB fee $10,000; Ramsey Lewis Trio fee $5,000; attendance about 3,300

events.title: Grandpa Jones and Lester Flatt at the Bluegrass Festival
events.body: Grandpa Jones entertained a crowd at the fine arts center amphitheatre during an ASG-sponsored Bluegrass Festival in the spring of 1978, with the Pinnacle Boys and Lester Flatt and the Nashville Grass also on the programme. The Herald reported on 25 April that the bluegrass crowds were relaxed and casual.

events.title: $23,000 of losses nearly cost ASG the concert programme
events.body: After ASG lost more than $23,000 on major concerts across the year, dean of student affairs Charles Keown recommended to the Board of Regents that its entertainment budget be halved for 1978-79 and that a committee study whether the University Center Board should take over programming. Bob Moore argued at the 29 April meeting that students would have less involvement if the change were made, and the regents voted to let ASG keep its full $62,000 entertainment budget while directing President Downing to appoint the study committee.
events.money: more than $23,000 lost on major concerts; $62,000 entertainment budget retained for 1978-79

events.title: ASG stops funding the Volunteer Bureau and starts a newsletter
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG had stopped funding the Student Volunteer Bureau and would start a newsletter. The bureau, which placed students in community volunteer work and in elementary school tutoring, had been part of ASG since January 1975.

events.title: Judicial Council denied Ed Johnson's election appeal
events.body: Losing candidate Ed Johnson contested the election result, and after a long debate the Associated Student Government Judicial Council denied his appeal. The ruling let Steve Thornton's win stand. While the case was pending the Herald had criticized the appeal system for a lack of objectivity.

events.title: Moore questioned freshman campaign spending and the Herald answered him
events.body: President Bob Moore publicly questioned how freshman class candidates were spending their campaign money, in a story the Herald headlined "A$G?". The paper answered the same week with an editorial arguing that Moore's comment was not good politics. Moore wrote back disputing the editorial.

executive.name: Cathy Murphy
executive.note: Elected on 12 April 1977 with 580 votes, defeating Jim Keffer's 446. She had written for ASG's own Student Insight supplement the previous April on the second cheque-cashing centre Steve Henry and Christy Vogt obtained at the College Heights Bookstore. The 1978 Talisman caption on the ASG meeting photograph calls her simply 'vice president'.
profile: Cathy Murphy ran for ASG administrative vice president in the April 1977 election and defeated Jim Keffer, 580 votes to 446, to take the office for 1977-78. The Herald's index for 26 September 1975 lists a report headlined "Roger Phelps, Cathy Murphy Elected to Top Freshman Offices," but the archive does not preserve the report itself, and the 1978 Talisman lists two students of that name, so whether the freshman officer and the ASG vice president were the same person is not established.

The year before her election she had written for ASG's own Student Insight supplement about the second cheque-cashing centre that outgoing officers Steve Henry and Christy Vogt had obtained for students at the College Heights Bookstore. In office, the 1978 Talisman's yearbook caption for a March 1978 ASG meeting shows her alongside president Bob Moore, activities vice president David Bass and secretary Sharon May at what the caption calls "a light moment"; the same yearbook page identifies her simply as vice president.

executive.name: Gary Reed
executive.note: Elected treasurer on 12 April 1977, defeating Georgiana Carlson 554 to 437.
profile: Gary Reed was elected ASG treasurer in the April 1977 election, defeating Georgiana Carlson 554 votes to 437, and served through 1977-78. The archive has not turned up further coverage of his time in the office.

executive.name: Sharon May
executive.note: Unopposed for secretary in the April 1977 election. The 1978 Talisman names her secretary in the caption to its ASG meeting photograph and indexes her as Sharon Gay May on that page.
profile: Sharon May ran unopposed for ASG secretary in the April 1977 election. The 1978 Talisman names her secretary in its caption to an ASG meeting photograph and separately indexes her, under a fuller form of her name, as Sharon Gay May. The same yearbook's caption for a March 1978 meeting places her at "a light moment" alongside president Bob Moore, vice president Cathy Murphy and activities vice president David Bass.

executive.name: Brent Shockley
executive.note: Elected activities vice president on 12 April 1977 with 532 votes, defeating Bill Cortus's 510. He does not appear in the office in any later source found here: by 24 January 1978 the Herald was naming David Bass as ASG activities vice president. The 1978 Talisman separately records Shockley, a Scottsville senior, spending the spring semester in Frankfort as one of 18 legislative interns, working for the Legislative Research Commission; the archive found no report stating why or when he left the office.
profile: Brent Shockley, a Scottsville senior studying government, was elected ASG activities vice president in the April 1977 election, defeating Bill Cortus 532 votes to 510. He does not appear in the office in any later source found in this archive: by 24 January 1978 the Herald was naming David Bass as ASG's activities vice president, and this archive has found no report of when or why Shockley left.

The 1978 Talisman explains where he went: that spring he was one of 18 university students who served as legislative interns in Frankfort, and he worked for the Legislative Research Commission preparing bill drafts and summaries and tracking where bills stood in the state Senate. "It's tedious and requires a lot of work," he told the yearbook, recalling being handed his own desk on his first day and thinking back to a sixth-grade field trip to the capitol.

executive.name: David Bass
executive.note: Named ASG activities vice president by the Herald from January 1978 and by the 1978 Talisman. He announced the signing of the Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick for 14 February 1978, and said ASG had decided against a free concert that spring, spreading the funds instead and charging students $3.50 for all major concerts. He said mini-concerts might stop being free so that better acts could be booked, but that ASG was trying to keep them free and to hold spending between $1,500 and $2,500. He handled the Average White Band and Ramsey Lewis Trio free concert of 18 April 1978.
profile: David Bass took over as ASG activities vice president after Brent Shockley left the post; the Herald was naming him to the office by 24 January 1978, and the 1978 Talisman also records him in it. He announced that ASG had signed the Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick for a 14 February 1978 show and said ASG had decided against giving a free concert that spring, spreading its entertainment funds across the season instead and charging students $3.50 for advance tickets to major concerts. He said ASG might stop offering free mini-concerts so it could book better acts, while trying to keep spending on them between $1,500 and $2,500.

Bass handled the year's one free show, the Average White Band and Ramsey Lewis Trio concert of 18 April 1978 and drew about 3,300 people. The 1978 Talisman's caption for a March 1978 ASG meeting photograph places him, president Bob Moore, secretary Sharon May and vice president Cathy Murphy together at what it calls "a light moment."

executive.name: Tricia Cook
executive.note: The 1978 Talisman records that a College Heights Herald editorial attacking ASG for inaction cited among its examples an inner-office joke at a congress meeting declaring the day 'Be Kind to Tricia Day' in honour of Cook, interim ASG secretary. The yearbook adds that several ASG members afterwards said the actions the editorial listed were not laughable. The volume does not say when or why the office became interim.
profile: Tricia Cook served as ASG's interim secretary for part of 1977-78; the 1978 Talisman does not say when or why the office became interim. The yearbook records that a College Heights Herald editorial attacking ASG for inaction cited, among its examples, an inner-office joke at a congress meeting declaring the day "Be Kind to Tricia Day" in Cook's honour. Several ASG members told the Talisman afterward that the actions the editorial had listed were not, in fact, laughable.

officers.name: Bob Tinsley
officers.note: Tinsley chaired the seven-member judicial council that on 17 April 1978 rejected Ed Johnson's challenge to Steve Thornton's 72-vote win. The council heard more than an hour of testimony, met privately and deadlocked; Tinsley did not vote the first time and broke the tie in Thornton's favour on the second. The council's report found it could not be proven that enough illegal votes were cast to change the election, and Johnson said he would carry the appeal no further.
profile: Bob Tinsley, of Radcliff, chaired ASG's seven-member Judicial Council in 1977-78. On 17 April 1978 the council, hearing more than an hour of testimony and then deliberating privately, rejected Ed Johnson's challenge to Steve Thornton's 72-vote win in that spring's presidential election; the panel deadlocked, and Tinsley, who had not voted on the first ballot, broke the tie in Thornton's favor on the second. The council's report found it could not be shown that enough illegal votes had been cast to change the outcome, and Johnson said he would take the appeal no further. Tinsley was also a member of WKU's Scabbard and Blade military honor society that year and defended the campus Rifle Corps in a Herald letter published 24 January 1978.

src2.label: 1976 Talisman, class listing

officers.office: Chairman, ASG Rules and Elections Committee
officers.name: Gene Saunders
officers.note: Saunders chaired the committee that ran the April 1978 election and first heard Ed Johnson's complaint. He said he had seen two poll workers wearing Thornton buttons and told both to take them off, that there was no basis to the complaint, and that his recommendation would be to allow the election. The committee rejected the protest and the judicial council then rejected the appeal.
profile: Gene Saunders chaired ASG's Rules and Elections Committee in 1977-78 and ran the April 1978 election that produced a formal protest: his committee was the first to hear Ed Johnson's complaint that poll workers had campaigned for candidate Steve Thornton by wearing his campaign buttons. Saunders told the Herald he had seen two workers wearing the buttons and told both to remove them, but found no basis for Johnson's complaint and recommended the election be allowed to stand; his committee rejected the protest, and the Judicial Council under Bob Tinsley rejected Johnson's appeal of that decision on 17 April 1978. Saunders had written the Herald repeatedly in the two years before taking the chairmanship: an April 1976 letter accused the paper of 'yellow journalism' in its ASG coverage, a companion letter the same month credited ASG resolutions with securing better intramural facilities, and a January 1977 letter proposed a student survey on dormitory visitation policy.

officers.name: John Grizzell
officers.note: Photographed in debate with representative Brad Ford during the long ASG argument over ratifying the Student Rights Alliance petition on dormitory rules, which Congress eventually voted to support. One member argued during the debate that recognising the alliance would be a potential threat to the ASG housing committee.
profile: John Grizzell chaired Associated Student Government's housing committee in 1977-78, during a year the Herald and the 1978 Talisman both covered as a running fight over dormitory rules. The Talisman's ASG section photographed Grizzell in debate with a representative named Brad Ford over ratifying the Student Rights Alliance's petition on dorm rules, a proposal Congress eventually voted to support; one member argued during the debate that recognizing the alliance posed a potential threat to ASG's own housing committee.

The same academic year, the Herald covered the wider dorm reform push in headlines like "American Civil Liberties Union Will Investigate Dorm Reform" (Nov. 1977) and "Dorm Reformers Lose Spirit, But Close Doors" (June 1978); ASG itself tabled and later voted on the dorm petition during this period, the same debate in which Grizzell's committee took part.

members.name: Brad Ford
members.note: Also captioned, with Gene Saunders, as an ASG committee chairman; the committee itself is not named in the source, so no separate committee record is entered.
profile: Ford was a Congress representative in 1977-78. The 1978 Talisman also captions him, alongside Gene Saunders, as an ASG committee chairman, without naming which committee he chaired.

members.name: Kevin Kinne
members.note: Indexed in the yearbook as Kevin Robert Kinne, p. 34.

leaders.name: Steven Thornton
leaders.note: Contested the ASG presidency against Ed Johnson in the 6 April 1978 election, campaigning on his experience; Johnson's contest of the result was denied by the Judicial Council on 18 April 1978 (see 1977-78 events, the outgoing Moore administration's year). This replaces a prior citation to 'Herald 54:54, 12 Apr 1979' - that issue is the following year's primary, does not name Thornton, and has been moved to 1979-80.

sources.label: WKU SGA, Former SGA Presidents roster, archived 24 Sep 2001

profile: Thornton beat Ed Johnson for the Associated Student Government presidency in the 6 April 1978 election, campaigning on his experience; Johnson contested the result, and the ASG Judicial Council denied his appeal on 18 April 1978 after a long debate.

In office that fall, Thornton's ASG tabled an open house bill rather than act on it, the Herald reported on 28 September 1978. By January 1979 the government faced a fight to keep control of student activities funding and was pressing for a student seat on a state-level council, both reported in the same 25 January 1979 issue.

In March 1979 the Herald reported Thornton and fellow WKU student Terri Craig elected to the executive council of the Student Government Association of Kentucky, a state-level body - the kind of state seat ASG had been pressing for two months earlier. In the last full week of his term, Thornton's ASG approved resolutions on campus housing and parking policy, reported 26 April 1979, the same week voting closed in the election for his successor. The archive does not otherwise show how the January activities-funding fight was resolved, and no further Herald coverage of the Thornton administration has been found before his successor, Jamie Hargrove, was profiled as the new ASG head at the start of the 1979-80 year.

events.title: President Dero Downing announces his resignation
events.body: Downing, who had led WKU since 1969, announced he would step down effective 31 December 1978. Vice President John Minton took over as interim president the following January while the Board of Regents searched for a successor.

events.title: ASG tables an open house bill
events.body: The Associated Student Government set aside a proposed open house bill rather than act on it, one of the fall semester's first pieces of business under new president Steven Thornton.

events.title: John Minton sworn in as interim president
events.body: Vice President John Minton was sworn in as WKU's interim president by Judge Charles Reynolds, succeeding Dero Downing and holding the post until Donald Zacharias took office that August.

events.title: ASG signs three lectures for the spring
events.body: The Associated Student Government signed three lectures for the spring semester, part of its ongoing role booking campus speakers.

events.title: ASG could lose control of activities funding
events.body: The Associated Student Government faced losing control over student activities funding, the Herald reported, a direct threat to one of the government's core powers.

events.title: ASG wants a student on a state council
events.body: In the same issue that reported the funding fight, the Associated Student Government pressed for a student seat on a state-level council, part of the broader campaign for student representation that ran through the decade.

events.title: ASG approves resolutions on housing and parking policy
events.body: In one of the outgoing Thornton administration's final acts, the Associated Student Government approved resolutions addressing campus housing and parking policy.

events.title: Roll-call votes made public; Moore ruled ineligible
events.body: ASG decided its roll-call votes would be made public, the Herald reported. The same issue reported that former president Bob Moore was ineligible for an Associated Student Government job.

events.title: David Rue wins freshman presidency by 11 votes
events.body: In the freshman election held under ASG, David Rue was elected president by 11 votes. Only 95 students had voted in the freshman primary the week before.

events.title: ASG backs Thornton's plan for minority representation
events.body: The Associated Student Government backed president Steve Thornton's plan to add minorities to the regents' presidential screening panel. The Herald's editorial page argued the regents should appoint a minority representative.

events.title: ASG approves revised constitution
events.body: The congress approved a revised Associated Student Government constitution. The revision capped a fall in which ASG also pushed teacher evaluations and parking rezoning.

events.title: ASG establishes a Minorities Board
events.body: ASG established a Minorities Board, the Herald reported. The move followed the fall's push to add minority voices to the presidential screening process.

events.title: Jamie Hargrove easily wins the presidency
events.body: The Herald reported that Jamie Hargrove easily won the Associated Student Government presidency, defeating David Young 1,087-535 on a turnout of 1,725 votes, up from 1,097 in the 1978 election. In the other executive races reported the same day, Steve Fuller defeated Tom Jecker 973-574 for administrative vice president, Dean Bates defeated Ben Bratcher 785-761 for activities vice president - the closest of the four races - Betty Thompson defeated Lynn Driver 1,052-517 for secretary, and Terri Craig defeated Darell Pierce 937-623 for treasurer.

events.title: ASG hands its concerts to an outside promoter
events.body: The Board of Regents gave ASG authority to seek outside help booking concerts, and ASG contracted Sunshine Promotions of Indianapolis, producers of a Rolling Stones show in Lexington that summer and of Summer Jam II in Louisville. The firm had booked more than 150 concerts; for its part of the bargain ASG was to receive 13 percent of the net profits. President Steve Thornton said at least three major concerts were being planned for the year.
events.money: ASG to take 13 percent of net profits

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 5, 7 September 1978

events.title: Player and Exile play the Homecoming concert
events.body: Player and Exile played Diddle Arena on Homecoming night to 4,296 people. Player, whose hits were "This Time I'm In It For Love" and "Baby Come Back," failed to get the crowd on its feet; Exile, from Richmond, skipped its sound check and played through poor sound but had the arena standing. After $24,000 in production costs and Western's 13 percent cut of a $25,694.29 after-tax gross, the Talisman recorded that there was little financial success to speak of.
events.money: $25,694.29 after-tax gross; $24,000 production costs; Western took 13 percent

events.title: The Herald tells ASG to quit the concert business
events.body: An unsigned Herald editorial said it was time ASG got out of the concert business, arguing that concert promotion had taken most of the organisation's time and effort and that ASG could not even hire a promoter competently. It cited excessive university demands, poor communication with Sunshine Promotions and the unsigned contract behind the Homecoming show. The same issue carried a reader's letter defending the concert as good.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 23, 9 November 1978

events.title: Joe Cocker drops out; Wet Willie takes his place
events.body: Joe Cocker, who had been announced to appear with the Outlaws at Diddle Arena on 5 December, cancelled his entire tour, and Sunshine Promotions signed the southern rock band Wet Willie in his place. Advertisements in that issue read "ASG and WKU Present" the Outlaws with special guest Wet Willie, 7:30 p.m., $6 in advance and $7 on the day of the show. The same meeting heard that Eleanor Smeal, president of the National Organization for Women, would speak on 7 December in Van Meter Auditorium.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 27, 28 November 1978

events.title: The Outlaws cancel after 242 tickets sell
events.body: Reaction to the advertising for the Outlaws and Wet Willie was so poor that only 242 tickets had been sold by the week of the show. When the Outlaws' manager heard the figure he cancelled on the spot, according to university programs coordinator Tim Nemeth. The December date, ASG's replacement for the Joe Cocker booking, never happened.

events.title: John Prine sells out Van Meter and ASG still loses $2,000
events.body: John Prine came to Western in the autumn of 1978 and did what no other musical act had done in a long time, playing to a capacity house. But Van Meter Auditorium holds only slightly more than 1,000, and even with a sellout and tickets priced higher than any previous mini-concert, ASG lost about $2,000 on the show. His five-man band ran through 25 songs, among them "Spanish Pipedream," "Dear Abby," "The Bottomless Lake" and "Sam Stone."

events.title: Eleanor Smeal's lecture keeps slipping
events.body: Activities vice president David Carwell told ASG's first meeting of the semester that the university was still trying to reschedule a lecture by Eleanor Smeal, president of the National Organization for Women, for February or March; she had been announced for 7 December and had not come. He set out what ASG was paying the three speakers it had signed: $4,000 for Dick Gregory, $2,000 for Princeton professor Gerard O'Neill and $2,000 for Congresswoman Shirley Chisholm, plus expenses, with all the lectures free. Carwell added that tickets for the Heart concert at Diddle Arena on 15 February would go on sale on 22 January at $7 in advance and $8 on the day.
events.money: Gregory $4,000; O'Neill $2,000; Chisholm $2,000; Heart tickets $7 advance, $8 day of show

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 33, 18 January 1979

events.title: Heart at Diddle Arena
events.body: Heart played Diddle Arena on 15 February with Ann Wilson opening on "High Times" and her sister Nancy on guitar, running through "Heartless," "Straight On," "Magazine," "Mistral Wind," "Dog and Butterfly," "Hijinx," "Crazy on You" and "Barracuda." Sunshine Promotions had signed the band as its first major break for Western, but only 5,821 came, a little more than half of capacity. Western made about $5,200 from the show, the one clear financial success of the concert year.

events.title: Forum '79 cut to one night
events.body: ASG's gubernatorial candidates' discussion panel, scheduled for two nights, was shortened to one after the university orchestra needed Van Meter Auditorium on the Monday. President Steve Thornton said the surviving session would run at 7:30 p.m. on the Tuesday, with Democrats Carroll Hubbard, Ralph Ed Graves and George Atkins appearing and Lieutenant Governor Thelma Stovall sending a representative. Ray White was the only Republican candidate willing to attend; Terry McBrayer and Louie Nunn stayed away.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 48, 27 March 1979

events.title: ASG's promoter had not signed a contract days before the Player and Exile concert
events.body: ASG said in the early autumn of 1978 that it would sign a contract with Sunshine Promotions, an Indianapolis concert firm, and its activities vice president David Carwell said the company met the three requirements for an outside promoter: an office within 500 miles of Western, at least 75 major concerts promoted, and $2 million grossed on them. Eight days before the Player and Exile concert of 3 November, the Herald reported that Western had still not signed, because the firm would not post the $100,000 performance bond the university required to guarantee that all the bills would be paid. Sunshine's Sybesma said Indiana insurance companies wanted 100 per cent collateral and a $2,000 service fee for the bond, and said his company might instead put up money before each concert. Sunshine later posted an irrevocable letter of credit that Western could cash if the concert bills went unpaid.

src.label: College Heights Herald 54:19, 26 Oct 1978; 1979 Talisman, Associated Student Government section

events.title: Gerald O'Neill on space colonies
events.body: Gerald O'Neill, a physics professor at Princeton and author of "The High Frontier", told 100 people in the Center Theater in his lecture of 2 April 1979 that space colonies and solar power stations were possible with current technology, and that electricity from solar cells could be sent back to Earth as low energy microwaves. He said plans for space colonies existed but President Carter had abolished the NASA office exploring space colonisation, and that he was concerned about the militarisation of space because Carter had signed a bill to develop a particle beam weapon to be placed in space. The same yearbook records that lectures and concerts had been run by Associated Student Government until the Board of Regents voted on 31 March 1979 to hand that programming to a new University Center Board from the following autumn.

src.label: 1979 Talisman, Lectures p. 97 and University Center Board p. 81

events.title: Shirley Chisholm closed the Black Awareness Symposium
events.body: Congresswoman Shirley Chisholm cancelled her February lecture, which is why the former Black Awareness Week was stretched across the spring semester as a symposium, and her rescheduled talk on 18 April closed it. She spoke on America's unfulfilled legacies before a crowd of about 250, predominantly black, who shouted and chanted in response, describing herself as a people's politician who could not be manipulated and saying she was there to tell people what they did not want to hear. The same yearbook records that lectures and concerts had been run by Associated Student Government until a reorganised University Center Board took them over in the autumn of 1979.

src.label: Talisman 1979, Black Awareness Symposium and lectures sections

events.title: The Regents take concerts and lectures away from ASG
events.body: The Board of Regents approved a rebuilt University Center Board on 31 March 1979 and funded it with $80,000 for programming. From the autumn its committees of students and administrators would run the lectures and concerts Associated Student Government had been running. ASG kept three seats, held by its president, its activities vice president and one member of congress, alongside representatives of the Interfraternity and Panhellenic councils, United Black Students, the men's and women's residence hall councils, two other students and three faculty members. The university programs coordinator, Tim Nemeth, said the new board would involve more student participation, and then put its maximum at ten students working on lectures and concerts against the fifty involved under ASG.
events.money: $80,000 to the University Center Board for programming

events.title: Colleagues accuse an ASG officer of neglecting his duties
events.body: The Herald reported on 7 December 1978, in a piece by Catherine Hancock headlined "Elusive Associated Student Government Officer Neglecting Duties, Colleagues Claim," that fellow ASG members accused officer David Carwell of not doing his job. The archive's index does not preserve enough of the article's text to confirm the specific allegations, Carwell's response, or how the matter was resolved.

events.title: Congress passes constitutional amendments
events.body: Tom Beshear reported in the Herald of 8 February 1979 that the Associated Student Government had passed constitutional amendments, ten weeks after Congress approved a revised constitution on 30 November 1978.

events.title: Thornton and Craig win seats on Kentucky's student government council
events.body: The Herald reported two Western students, ASG president Steven Thornton and Terri Craig, elected to the executive council of the Student Government Association of Kentucky, a state-level student body - the kind of state seat ASG had pressed for in January. The same issue editorialized that ASG should make its teacher evaluations public.

events.title: Voting held for Thornton's successor; candidates lean on experience
events.body: Students voted in the ASG general election to choose Thornton's successor, with the Herald reporting the presidential candidates relying on their experience. The Herald ran candidate endorsements the same day, including United Black Students' backing of Jamie Hargrove, and pieces from outgoing president Steve Thornton and former president Bob Moore.

executive.name: David Young
executive.note: Elected unopposed in April 1978, having been a representative from Ogden College that year; he told the Herald his main goal as an executive officer would be to begin a book exchange. In spring 1979 he explained the new constitution's creation of 24 separate races for the 24 representative-at-large seats on ASG congress as a way to make candidates compete head to head.
profile: David Young, a representative from Ogden College in 1977-78, ran unopposed for ASG administrative vice president in the April 1978 election. He told the Herald his main goal as an executive officer would be to start a book exchange for students.

In office he helped shepherd a new ASG constitution, approved by congress in November 1978 and ratified by the student body at the April 1979 elections, which created 24 separate races for the 24 representative-at-large seats on congress. Young told the 1979 Talisman the change was meant to "force some heads-up competition" between candidates rather than let them run in blocs.

executive.name: Steve Shipp
executive.note: One of the four executive officers elected unopposed in the April 1978 election; the Herald's results report names him treasurer.
profile: Steve Shipp was one of four ASG executive officers elected unopposed in the April 1978 election; the Herald's results report names him treasurer for 1978-79. The archive has not turned up further coverage of his time in the office.

executive.name: Alice Wicks
executive.note: Elected unopposed in April 1978. She told the Herald before the vote that she wanted to make students more aware of ASG's functions and that she was joining ASG because she wanted to get more involved in student government.
profile: Alice Wicks ran unopposed for ASG secretary in the April 1978 election. Before the vote she told the Herald she wanted to make students more aware of what ASG actually did, and that she had joined the organization because she wanted to be more involved in student government.

executive.name: David Carwell
executive.note: Elected unopposed in April 1978 and put in charge of concerts, saying he wanted more mini-concerts and fewer big shows. In the autumn he said the Indianapolis firm Sunshine Promotions met Western's three tests for an outside promoter, but shortly before the 3 November Player and Exile concert it emerged that the contract had never been signed, Sunshine having refused a $100,000 performance bond; it later posted a letter of credit instead. He also chaired ASG's lecture and concert committees. On 7 December 1978 the Herald reported colleagues' claims that he was neglecting the duties of an office that carried $800 a year, that he had missed five ASG meetings, and that lecture committee members and a Herald reporter could not reach him; president Steve Thornton said one more missed meeting would take him before the executive council to explain, and Carwell replied that much of his work was done on the telephone from home and defended his record. This archive found no later report of an executive council hearing, of any removal, or of a successor in the office.
profile: David Carwell was elected ASG activities vice president unopposed in the April 1978 election and put in charge of the year's concerts and lectures, saying he wanted more mini-concerts and fewer large shows. That fall ASG moved to sign the Indianapolis firm Sunshine Promotions as an outside concert promoter; Carwell told the 1979 Talisman that Sunshine met the university's three tests for such a firm, having an office within 500 miles of Western, having promoted at least 75 major concerts, and having grossed at least $2 million on them. Shortly before the 3 November 1978 Player and Exile concert it emerged that the contract with Sunshine had never actually been signed, because the firm balked at a $100,000 performance bond; Sunshine later posted a letter of credit instead.

On 7 December 1978 the Herald reported colleagues' claims that Carwell was neglecting an office that carried an $800 salary, saying he had missed five ASG meetings and that lecture committee members and a Herald reporter had been unable to reach him. President Steve Thornton said one more missed meeting would bring him before the executive council to explain himself; Carwell replied that much of his work was done by telephone from home and defended his record. This archive has found no later report of an executive council hearing, of any removal, or of a successor taking the office before the year ended. That spring the Board of Regents voted to move some responsibility for lecture and concert programming out of ASG's hands and into a rebuilt University Center Board, effective that fall.

officers.name: Victor Jackson
officers.note: Jackson chaired the committee behind the student evaluation of faculty that ASG approved, a form called the Purdue Cafeteria System in which teachers pick questions from a list of several hundred around a common core. He said only the core questions would be made public because of printing costs, and put the cost at about $6,500 in the first year and about $5,000 a year after; the evaluations were scheduled to begin in the fall 1979 semester. He had earlier been the only black student running in the campus election for the Board of Regents' presidential screening committee.
profile: Victor Jackson, an accounting major from Clarksville, Tennessee, chaired ASG's faculty evaluation committee in 1978-79. That year ASG approved a questionnaire for a student evaluation of the faculty, called the Purdue Cafeteria System, under which instructors chose questions from a list of several hundred, each form built around a set of core questions common to all of them. Jackson said only the core questions would be published, citing printing costs, and put the first year's cost at about $6,500 and about $5,000 a year after; the evaluations were due to begin in fall 1979.

Jackson had earlier been the only Black student to run in a campus election for a seat on the Board of Regents' presidential screening committee, an October 1978 vote called after roughly forty Black students, most of them members of the campus NAACP chapter and the United Black Students, asked ASG to secure minority representation on the committee. Two students were to be chosen for the committee in a campus election, and NAACP chapter president Anita Orr said at the October meeting that Jackson had little chance of winning, since minority students made up only about 6.5 percent of the student body. The regents in the end appointed a Black elementary school principal from Russellville and a female WKU associate professor of home economics and family living to the committee, at the request of ASG president and student regent Steve Thornton. The 1979 Talisman also credits Jackson with serving on several ASG committees that year and being, in the words of Herald reporter Tom Beshear, 'very active.'

officers.name: Bob Moore
officers.note: Nominated and accepted as Judicial Council chairman at ASG's first meeting of the year, 29 August 1978. This is Robert "Bob" Moore, ASG president 1977-78. The Herald reported 7 September 1978 that the former president was ruled ineligible for an Associated Student Government job; by the 12 September 1978 meeting Thornton announced an opening for Judicial Council chairman and Congress confirmed Steve Wilson in the position, 30 in favour with 3 abstaining. Neither source explicitly ties the two events, but the dates align and no other ASG post for Moore is recorded that year.
profile: Bob Moore, who had just finished a one-year term as Associated Student Government president, was nominated and accepted as Judicial Council chairman at ASG's first meeting of the year, 29 August 1978.

The Herald reported on 7 September 1978 that the former president had been ruled ineligible for an Associated Student Government job. By the 12 September meeting, an opening for Judicial Council chairman had appeared and Congress confirmed Steve Wilson in the position, 30 votes in favour with 3 abstaining. Neither source explicitly ties the ineligibility ruling to the chairmanship, but the dates align and no other ASG post for Moore is recorded that year, so his tenure as chairman appears to have run under two weeks.

profile: Steve Wilson was confirmed as chairman of Associated Student Government's Judicial Council at the 12 September 1978 Congress meeting, on a vote of 30 in favour with 3 abstaining, after president Steven Thornton announced the position open. The Herald's 14 September 1978 issue reported the appointment under the headline "Judicial Council Chairman Picked." He took the post from Bob Moore, the former ASG president whose brief hold of the chairmanship that same fall is separately recorded; no source connects Moore's departure to the opening Thornton announced. The archive has not turned up further coverage of Wilson's time in the post.

documents.title: ASG minutes, 29 August 1978
documents.summary: Minutes of the Associated Student Government's first meeting of the 1978-79 year, under President Steve Thornton. Committee reports cover concerts and lectures, dorm reassignments, a new student discount card, and the summer class schedule; Congress accepted nominees for the Judicial Council and appointed two members to the Rules and Elections Committee.
documents.extract: The Associated Student Government ... held its first meeting August 29, 1978.

documents.summary: Committee reports on the fall concert series (Southern Star, John Prine), the Student Discount Card and a Bill 78-2 debate on roll call votes, which passed unanimously. Congress appointed Rita Young to represent the College of Education.
documents.extract: Steve Thornton moved that Rita Young be appointed ... from the College of Education.
