profile: Leslie Bedo, a senior corporate communications major from Bowling Green, served as SGA president for 2001-02 after three years in the organization, having previously been parliamentarian, public relations committee chair and executive vice president. Her stated priorities for the year were tuition, student health and online course syllabi, and she described SGA as run "by the students, for the students."

As student regent, Bedo pushed back in August 2001 when the Board of Regents raised tuition 9 percent at a meeting held before fall classes officially began. She said the timing sent "a message to students" that the increase would pass before they could weigh in, though she ultimately joined the board's unanimous vote approving it.

That November, Bedo wrote a Herald op-ed titled "Meeting Goals of Student Government Association, But Not Students'", questioning the organization's effectiveness; fellow member Troy Ransdell responded in the same issue with a piece headlined "Action, Not Complaints." The same paper reported SGA was buying Christmas presents for children at Potter Children's Home that season.

In March 2002, near the end of her term, Bedo publicly challenged the university after a land deal meant to add 400 to 500 parking spaces fell through while the Diddle Arena renovation was removing about 200 spaces. She noted regents had raised the student athletics fee on the expectation of more parking, said "the parking has been put on hold," and called added parking imperative because more students parked on campus than attended basketball games.

As her term wound down, an April 30, 2002 Herald profile by Molly O'Connor reported renewed interest in SGA under Bedo's leadership. Jamie Sears was elected to succeed her that April; Bedo's own former rival for vice president of administration, Patti Johnson, went on to become SGA president herself in a September 2004 special election.

events.title: Bedo questions timing of 9 percent tuition increase, then votes for it
events.body: WKU's Board of Regents voted on Friday, August 17 to raise tuition 9 percent starting in fall 2002, the first tuition hike in university history devoted entirely to faculty and staff pay. Student Regent Leslie Bedo said she was troubled that the vote came before students officially began fall classes, telling the board it sent a message that the university would slide the increase through before students could respond. Despite her concerns, Bedo joined the unanimous vote approving the increase, which raised in-state undergraduate tuition $138 a semester, from $1,422 to $1,560.

events.title: Regents approve $32.5 million Diddle Arena bond deal funded by student athletics fee
events.body: The Board of Regents approved an agreement with the City of Bowling Green to sell up to $32.5 million in bonds to renovate E.A. Diddle Arena, with the university repaying the debt service through its student athletics fee. Planned improvements included air conditioning, new seating, luxury boxes, expanded parking and a pedway from new parking areas to the arena. The renovation was scheduled to run from April to September 2002.

events.title: Students organize candlelight vigil after September 11 attacks
events.body: Two days after the September 11 attacks, WKU held a student-organized candlelight vigil at the Ivan Wilson Fine Arts Center Amphitheater as part of a slate of campus responses. The university also planned a faculty forum at Van Meter Auditorium, opened the Faculty House for reflection and counseling, created a condolences message board to send to New York and Washington, and scheduled a blood drive for September 27.

events.title: SGA raises over $800 for Red Cross disaster relief
events.body: The SGA homepage, as archived on November 6, 2001, reported that the association had helped raise more than $800 for the Red Cross Disaster Relief Fund following the September 11 attacks. The same page announced that Congress applications were available in DUC 130 and promoted the Campus Spirit Award, which SGA administered that year.

events.title: Provide-A-Ride carries 929 passengers over twelve fall nights
events.body: SGA's Provide-A-Ride service posted its fall 2001 ridership on its website, listing twelve Thursday and Friday nights of operation between September 20 and November 9, 2001. Nightly passenger counts ranged from 49 to 112, for a total of 929 riders over the period.

events.title: Fall project slate: online syllabi, extended library hours, alcohol policy
events.body: SGA's current-projects page, as archived on November 27, 2001, listed the association's work for the semester. Projects included online course syllabi, extended library hours during finals week, a review of the alcohol policy, a 9/11 Remembrance Wall, the SGA Disaster Relief Fund, Provide-A-Ride keychains, the Senior Class Challenge, the Campus Spirit Award, Homecoming Queen 2001 and the Homecoming parade.

events.title: SGA organized Christmas presents for Potter Children's Home
events.body: The Herald reported that SGA was collecting Christmas presents that fall for children at Potter Children's Home, a Bowling Green residential care facility, in a news piece by staff writer Hollan Holm.

events.title: President Bedo and senator Ransdell publicly debated SGA's effectiveness
events.body: The same Herald issue ran dueling opinion pieces on SGA: an op-ed by President Leslie Bedo headlined "Meeting Goals of Student Government Association, But Not Students'", followed by a response from fellow member Troy Ransdell titled "Action, Not Complaints." The full text of the exchange is not available online; only the headlines and bylines are indexed.

events.title: SGA constitution amended, Spring 2002
events.body: TopSCHOLAR's SGA collection holds a copy of the WKU Student Government Association constitution described as "amended Spring 2002," indicating the association revised its governing document during Bedo's term. The specific amendments are not detailed in the record.

events.title: Herald profile reported renewed interest in SGA as Bedo's term ended
events.body: With Bedo's term winding down, the Herald ran a profile by Molly O'Connor headlined "Student Government Association President Sees Renewed Interest in Organization." The full article text is not available online; only the headline and byline are indexed.

events.title: Bedo presses parking issue after WKU land purchase collapses
events.body: Negotiations for WKU to buy the Forest Park Trailer Park for 400 to 500 new parking spaces broke down over price, even as the Diddle Arena renovation was set to eliminate about 200 spaces permanently. SGA President Leslie Bedo said several regents had voted to increase the student athletics fee on the basis that student parking would grow, and that the promised parking expansion had been put on hold. She argued more students parked on campus than attended basketball games and called more parking imperative.

events.title: Jamie Sears elected SGA president for 2002-03
events.body: In online voting, junior public relations major Jamie Sears of Melber defeated senior Sam Stinson 1,284 to 594 for SGA president, winning the seat as student representative on the Board of Regents. John Bradley beat Dana Lockhart 1,065 to 730 for executive vice president, Ross Pruitt ran unopposed for vice president of finance with 1,524 votes, Anna Coats edged Holly Skidmore 933 to 809 for vice president of public relations, and Brandon Copeland defeated Patti Johnson 1,106 to 761 for vice president of administration.

events.title: Voters approve Supremacy Clause constitutional amendment
events.body: SGA's official general election results page, archived on April 26, 2002, recorded that a constitutional amendment titled Supremacy Clause passed in the spring 2002 general election. The page listed the amendment result alongside the vote totals for the five executive races.

events.title: $2,000 renews the Campus Spirit Award

leaders.name: Jamie Sears
leaders.note: Confirmed in the College Heights Herald's own election headline, which ran the week she won.

sources.label: College Heights Herald 77:51, 11 Apr 2002 - "Jamie Sears Wins Election in Landslide" (O'Connor, Molly)

profile: Sears, a junior public relations major from Melber, won the presidency in a landslide, defeating senior Sam Stinson 1,284 votes to 594 in the April 2002 general election that also seated her incoming executive team: John Bradley as executive vice president, Ross Pruitt as vice president of finance, Anna Coats as vice president of public relations, and Brandon Copeland as vice president of administration.

Sears opened her 2002-03 term as SGA president under immediate scrutiny. Seventeen months after congress passed a bill putting about $5,000 of leftover budget money toward an on-campus gazebo, members discovered the gazebo was never built and the money was gone. When three members petitioned congress in September over $28,000 they said was unaccounted for, Sears told the Herald, "I have absolutely no idea where that money went." The petition was withdrawn only after her executive council created an ad hoc financial review committee.

By October the money had been traced: it had slipped back into SGA's general fund and been spent on other things, including computers for the SGA office. Sears acknowledged that she and former student activities director Scott Taylor had decided during the summer where the leftover money, which included the gazebo funds, would be allocated, saying other executive council members were consulted through email. She said the financial review committee would explain the budget findings to congress, and no move was made to set aside new gazebo money.

Sears finished the year on stronger footing. She traveled with about 20 Western students to Frankfort to oppose state budget cuts to higher education, calling the trip one of SGA's greatest accomplishments: "That was a great feeling seeing students from everywhere rallying for the same cause." Under her leadership congress debated more than 55 pieces of legislation and passed the first student referendum in SGA history, a $3 fee for radio station Revolution 91.7 that students approved in the spring election. Her final meeting as president came on April 22, 2003.

events.title: Members demand answers on missing gazebo money
events.body: SGA members Brooke Smith, Dana Lockhart and Sam Stinson petitioned congress over $28,000 they said was unaccounted for, including about $5,000 that a April 2001 bill had set aside to build an on-campus gazebo that never appeared. President Jamie Sears said of the gazebo fund, "I have absolutely no idea where that money went." The petition was withdrawn after the executive council formed an ad hoc financial review committee.

events.title: Herald editorial blasts SGA over 'Gazebo-Gate'
events.body: The Herald's 11-member editorial board attacked SGA leaders over what it called "Gazebo-Gate," saying the money had gone to computers for the SGA office instead of the promised gazebo. It called leaders' ignorance about the missing money "shameful" and challenged Sears by name to "do her job" and provide real answers, writing that "I don't know" did not cut it.

events.title: Gazebo funds traced to SGA general fund
events.body: Vice president of finance Ross Pruitt reported that the $13,000 SGA had put toward the gazebo mistakenly went back into the organization's general fund and was spent on other things, including computers for SGA. Sears said she and former student activities director Scott Taylor decided over the summer where the leftover budget money would go, with other executive council members consulted by email. Pruitt said leaders from the past two administrations shared the blame, saying "I didn't do my homework."

events.title: Congress votes down enrollment cap resolution
events.body: SGA congress rejected by a large margin a resolution asking Western to implement an enrollment cap, with Sears among those calling the measure too drastic. The failed proposal argued the university and state budgets had not kept pace with enrollment growth from 14,543 students in 1997 to about 17,770. Provost Barbara Burch and President Ransdell both said a cap was not the best answer to the growth problem.

events.title: Three resolutions pass on faculty pay, enrollment, parking
events.body: SGA passed two resolutions responding to a shortage of 75 faculty members and the lowest-paid faculty in the state, asking that unbudgeted tuition surplus money, about $800,000 that year, be used to hire faculty, and encouraging President Ransdell to create a task force on enrollment. A third resolution requested a change to the policy that gave Hilltopper Athletic Foundation donors student parking spaces, including the Grise Hall lot, at basketball games.

events.title: Freshman committee appointments tabled
events.body: SGA tabled Sears's proposal to appoint three freshmen, Tim Howard, Katie Dawson and Robert Watkins, as the student members of a joint University Senate and SGA enrollment growth committee. Sears said she picked freshmen so they could serve the committee's expected two to three year life, but critics including associate justice Dana Lockhart said the appointments would make it hard for SGA to be taken seriously.

events.title: SGA joins Frankfort rally against budget cuts
events.body: About 200 students from six public universities rallied at the state Capitol against cuts to higher education, after the Kentucky House passed a budget cutting Western's funding by more than $1 million. Western sent a delegation of roughly 20 people including SGA members, organized through the board of Kentucky's student body presidents. Sears said 17 people "took the initiative to get on the bus."

events.title: Congress puts $3 radio fee referendum on ballot
events.body: SGA unanimously approved a bill placing a referendum on the April 2-3 general election ballot letting students vote on a $3 student fee for campus radio station Revolution 91.7-WWHR, which was operating on a $7,000 budget unchanged since 1998. Executive vice president John Bradley, who championed the measure, said it would empower students and boost voter turnout. A yes vote would send the fee recommendation to the Board of Regents for a final decision.

events.title: Bradley elected president; 2,014 vote
events.body: A total of 2,014 students voted in the spring SGA election, with results announced shortly after 1 a.m. Friday by chief justice Holly Skidmore. Paducah junior John Bradley won the presidency unopposed with 1,662 votes, Patti Johnson beat Dana Lockhart 1,185 to 685 for executive vice president, and Jessica Martin beat Shawn Peavie 1,056 to 686 for vice president of administration. The $3 WWHR radio fee referendum passed 1,066 to 765 and moved to the Board of Regents.

events.title: SGA closes year after 55 pieces of legislation
events.body: SGA held its last meeting of the year on April 22, having heard and debated more than 55 pieces of legislation, including a resolution that earmarked funds for new benches across campus. Sears counted the Frankfort rally among the year's greatest accomplishments, and the Revolution 91.7 fee measure stood as the first student referendum in SGA history, awaiting a final Board of Regents vote on May 9. President-elect Bradley said the high election turnout was the semester's best moment and pledged to fight student apathy the next year.

events.title: Congress forms financial review committee, approves archivist bill
events.body: Five days after members petitioned over the missing gazebo funds, congress unanimously approved campus-improvements chair Nick Todd to lead the new ad hoc Financial Review Committee and Brooke Smith as parliamentarian. Congress also passed Bill 02-02-F, sponsored by executive vice president John Bradley, creating a student position to serve as SGA's archivist, and swore in two new members as the body's membership reached 71.

events.title: Record enrollment of 17,500 strains campus
events.body: Western opened the fall with enrollment ballooning to 17,500, nearly 1,000 more students than the year before and a 20 percent increase since 1997. President Gary Ransdell warned that growth would be "painful" amid decreased state funding, and the Board of Regents approved a 10.4 percent tuition increase for 2003-04.

events.title: $400 to rebuild the volleyball court in the Valley
events.body: Bill 02-04-F allocated $400 for sand, liner and wood borders to rebuild the volleyball court in front of Gilbert Hall. Nick Todd wrote it, arguing the court was in severe disrepair and residents had stopped using it.

executive.name: Ross Pruitt
profile: Ross Pruitt took office as vice president of finance for 2002-03, his candidacy covered in the Herald's election issue of 28 March 2002. That autumn he found himself at the center of what the Herald's editorial board branded "Gazebo-Gate": the $13,000 SGA had put toward an on-campus gazebo, authorized by a 2001 bill, had instead gone back into the organization's general fund and been spent on other things including office computers, discovered only after members petitioned Congress in September 2002. Reporting the finding to the Herald on 1 October 2002, Pruitt said past leaders had not properly earmarked the money and that year's executive council had spent it without knowing what it was, and that responsibility ran across his own council and those of the previous two years, including former presidents Leslie Bedo and Cassie Martin. Of his own part in it, he said he had not done his homework.

profile: Brandon Copeland, of Bardstown, won the 2002 race for vice president of administration; the Herald's election issue of 28 March 2002 profiled him alongside four other candidates under the headline "Five Dreamers, One Dream," and he thanked voters in a Herald letter on 9 April 2002.

After graduating, Copeland was one of three former SGA officers, with former Judicial Council justice Dana Lockhart and former information-technology director Matthew Pava, who wrote to the Herald on 26 August 2004 objecting to remarks Nick Todd made in the paper's 24 August issue, following Todd's resignation of the SGA presidency that summer. The three, writing as alumni who had served with Todd, said they were dismayed by his conduct and defended fellow former officer Jessica Martin against what they called unfounded criticism. leaders.name: John Bradley
leaders.note: Presided over the 2004 Constitutional Convention that created the three-branch structure. Quoted in Herald coverage of the investigation into his successor-elect.
profile: Bradley, a Paducah junior and sitting executive vice president, ran unopposed for SGA president in spring 2003, campaigning alongside Jessica Martin and Dana Lockhart on parking, keeping the cost of education low and making campus friendlier to students with disabilities. He counted the WWHR radio-fee student referendum among his accomplishments as executive vice president, and said he had worked to "depolarize the organization." As president he would also serve as the student member of the Board of Regents.

He opened the fall 2003 semester by naming low education costs his top priority, opposing plans to pass Greek Village land costs on to all students, and steering SGA toward campus safety after serving on the summer's Campus Safety Task Force. He launched an SGA Ambassador Council to visit student organizations weekly and scheduled the semester's first forum on campus safety.

events.title: The Constitutional Convention rebuilds the body
events.body: Three branches - Executive Cabinet, Senate and Judicial Council - drawn from the student body at large. The most consequential clause is the quietest: every enrolled student became a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections.

events.title: The president-elect was investigated before he took office
events.body: The Herald reported that Nick Todd, SGA's president-elect and vice president of finance, was suspected of misusing more than $600 through food purchases from an SGA Dining Dollars account, and that the allegation could jeopardize his status as president-elect; Todd could not be reached for comment despite repeated attempts. Articles of impeachment were drafted against his existing finance post, but the judicial council found the two-week process could not finish before the term ended. Because state law governs the student regent seat, the new constitution required a separate special election to fill it.

events.title: Bradley opens the year with cost, safety and involvement goals
events.body: New SGA president John Bradley opened the fall by naming low education costs his first goal and warning that fees for the proposed Greek Village should not be passed to the whole student body. SGA created an Ambassador Council to visit student organizations weekly, and planned its first forum of the semester on campus safety, an issue Bradley had worked on as a member of the Campus Safety Task Force formed after the death of freshman Katie Autry. The first congress meeting of the semester was set for August 26 in Downing University Center.

events.title: SGA lines up against plus/minus grading
events.body: SGA members voiced concern at their Tuesday meeting over a plus/minus grading system proposed in the University Senate by economics professor Brian Strow. Bradley said he planned to oppose it, reporting that the state's other student body presidents had urged him to fight it, and the Academic Affairs committee prepared a student questionnaire on the change. Chief Justice Troy Ransdell argued the system would penalize students who scored best.

events.title: Congress urged students to vote as the grading petition circulated
events.body: SGA unanimously passed a resolution at its Tuesday meeting recommending that Western's students vote in the Nov. 4 state election and research the candidates' stands on higher education. Bowling Green sophomore Robert Watkins, an SGA member and the author of the legislation, moved to suspend the by-laws so the resolution could pass before the vote. Members also reported that the petition against plus/minus grading had gathered 350 signatures with more petitions in circulation, and SGA planned a Homecoming tent on the Downing University Center south lawn.

events.title: SGA organizes for a higher education rally in Frankfort
events.body: SGA prepared to join student governments from across Kentucky at a February 5 rally at the state Capitol against cuts to higher education funding, with slogans such as "Don't Balance the Budget on Our Backs" and students asked to wear backpacks. Congress approved $650 for transportation and reserved 47 spots for the trip. Bradley conceded change that year might be "unreasonable" to expect but said rallying could affect the future.

events.title: SGA budget frozen as Western absorbed $5.6 million in cuts
events.body: SGA announced at its Tuesday meeting that its budget, along with the Campus Activities Board's, had been informally frozen while Western worked out how to cut the $5.6 million ordered by Gov. Ernie Fletcher's administration; the two groups would spend no money until President Gary Ransdell presented his budget cut plan to the Board of Regents. SGA held $65,309.52 in its 2003-04 budget at the time, plus about $7,400 in an Aramark contract and foundation accounts that were not affected. Bradley said congress could still pass legislation requiring money, with the director of student activities deciding whether funds were available.

events.title: Nick Todd elected SGA president as 1,232 students vote
events.body: Vice president of finance Nick Todd won the SGA presidency with 772 votes to Jessica Martin's 424, in a two-day online election in which 1,232 students voted. Katie Dawson won executive vice president with 778 votes and Evelina Petkova won administrative vice president with 692, with the first elected senate under the new constitution chosen at the same time. Bradley said he was disappointed by the turnout, and the winners were set to be sworn in at the SGA banquet on April 27.

events.title: Congress buys stepping stones for muddy campus paths
events.body: SGA unanimously approved legislation allocating $200 from its campus improvements account for stepping stones near Mass Media and Technology Hall, Tate Page Hall and Southwest Hall, where student foot traffic had worn dirt and mud paths. The bill's authors, Shawn Peavie and Sarah Cecil, said sidewalks had been considered but were too expensive. In the same meeting a straw poll on a proposed dorm Internet service fee drew 3 votes in support, 11 against and 11 abstentions.

events.title: SGA races to spend its remaining $45,000
events.body: With about $45,000 left of its original $105,000 budget for 2003-04, SGA moved to spend the remainder before the semester ended, since leftover funds would go to offset budget cuts across the university rather than carry over. Officers attributed the surplus partly to frugality during the spring budget freeze, and Todd suggested putting the money toward campus improvements such as benches or shuttle shelters. SGA also sponsored a dining services forum that week with Auxiliary Services and Dining Services officials.

events.title: Greek Village debate opens at SGA meeting
events.body: Students began voicing opinions about the proposed Greek Village, and how it might be paid for, at a Student Government Association meeting. The Herald reported some saw the project as a way to bring Greeks together while others called it a waste of money.

events.title: SGA proposes campus safety commission
events.body: Campus improvements committee chair Shawn Peavie, a Monticello junior, announced that SGA was looking into creating a campus safety commission. The commission would test safety measures ranging from checking locks to recording emergency response times.

events.title: IT vice president asks SGA to cut directory data
events.body: Richard Kirchmeyer, vice president for Information Technology, told SGA at its Tuesday meeting that some personal student information should be removed from the print and online campus directory to protect against identity theft. SGA weighed whether to adopt the recommendations.

events.title: SGA takes up $8,000 shuttle shelter legislation
events.body: Legislation requesting $8,000 for a shuttle bus shelter at the Jones-Jaggers stop was set for SGA's next meeting. Executive Vice President Patti Johnson said the Campus Improvements Committee brought it forward. Approval of student representatives to the University Senate was also on the agenda.

events.title: SGA unanimously passes legislation against plus/minus grading
events.body: SGA unanimously passed legislation at its Tuesday meeting objecting to a proposed plus/minus grading system. Economics professor Brian Strow was to formally propose the system to the University Senate that day.

events.title: SGA escalates plus/minus fight to rally and donors
events.body: SGA President John Bradley said the association would use all its possible tools to stop the plus/minus grading proposal, including a rally and meetings with university donors. The escalation followed SGA's passage of legislation opposing the system.

events.title: SGA demands two weeks notice on dining service changes
events.body: SGA unanimously passed legislation calling on Dining Services to give students more notification of changes to service hours or facilities. The resolution recommended that changes be posted and advertised at least two weeks before taking effect.

events.title: Correction clarifies Bradley stance on student regent tuition votes
events.body: The Herald corrected a front-page misquotation of SGA President John Bradley. There was a consensus among Kentucky student government presidents that student regents should not vote for tuition increases, but Bradley said he had never personally committed to withholding such a vote.

events.title: Plus/minus petition passes 1,500 signatures as Senate votes
events.body: The SGA-backed petition against the plus/minus grading system had gathered more than 1,500 signatures and SGA prepared a student rally. The University Senate was expected to vote on the system that afternoon in Garrett Ballroom, with supporters ready to defend it.

events.title: SGA resolution seeks advance notice of class cancellations
events.body: SGA unanimously passed a resolution at its Tuesday meeting recommending that academic departments notify students of class cancellations an hour and a half before the class was scheduled to meet.

events.title: SGA asks that student addresses in directories be optional
events.body: SGA passed a resolution on Tuesday asking the university to make access to student addresses in the printed and online directories optional. The legislation stated that students' permission should be obtained before their personal information is published.

events.title: SGA budget to fall by up to $17,000
events.body: SGA expected a $15,000 to $17,000 decrease in its 2004-2005 budget as part of university-wide cuts. SGA vice president Nick Todd announced the reduction at Tuesday's meeting, and the Herald reported it could affect the campus improvements committee and organizational aid.

events.title: Editorial faults students after 132 of 18,000 vote
events.body: A Herald editorial criticized student participation in SGA after only 132 of about 18,000 students voted on the organization's new constitution. The editorial contrasted that figure with the 86 percent of citizens who voted in South Africa's 1999 general elections.

events.title: Todd publicly denies financial impropriety
events.body: Nick Todd for the first time publicly addressed the allegations against him, denying any wrongdoing through a statement on Tuesday. The Herald quoted him saying he felt he had done nothing wrong.

events.title: Todd sworn in as president with investigation unresolved
events.body: Nick Todd was sworn in as SGA president at the association's banquet on Tuesday. Outgoing president John Bradley passed along a purple stress ball and other trinkets he had collected during his presidency.

events.title: Campus safety forum in DUC 305
events.body: President John Bradley opened SGA's campus safety forum on 11 September 2003 in Downing University Center room 305, taking questions from the floor and from students who had emailed. Chief Deane, Captain Wallace, Dean Howard Bailey and Dr Tice answered on the police escort service, crosswalks after a pedestrian was struck on University Boulevard, and unlit paths behind Rhodes-Harlin and McCormack.

events.title: $2,012.50 of giveaways to make SGA visible
events.body: Bill 03-02-F allocated up to $2,012.50 for more than 4,750 promotional items, pens, note pads, sweets, lanyards and flashlight keychains, all carrying the SGA name. They were given away at SGA Day, at JUMP tables and at other events, and a follow-up bill added $65 in November when the supplier had underquoted.

events.title: Organizational Aid reaches $19,000
events.body: Bill 03-04-F disbursed $19,000 in Organizational Aid, spread across dozens of registered organisations and the largest Organizational Aid payout this archive holds for the decade. Awards ran from $50 to Beta Gamma Sigma up to $425 for Amazing Tones of Joy and $400 for the Black Student Alliance, and SGA took sponsorship credit under its bylaws for every event the grants paid for.

events.title: Bill proposes an SGA Adopt-A-Tree Program
events.body: SGA's own legislation archive lists Bill 03-12-F, "SGA Adopt-A-Tree Program," dated 17 November 2003, among the fall 2003 session's bills. The archive page is an index of titles and dates only; it does not show whether the bill passed.

events.title: Buy-A-Book gets a publicity campaign
events.body: Bill 04-07-S committed SGA to promote the Buy-A-Book programme through Channel 12, Revolution 91.7, the SGA website, campus kiosks, residence halls and organisation mailboxes. The authors wrote it because students had complained they never heard about the scholarship.

events.title: Buy-A-Book applications close for spring 2004
events.body: Applications for the Buy-A-Book service were due in the SGA office at 130 Downing University Center by 4 p.m. on Friday 23 April 2004. Each award was $100 spent only on books at the College Heights Bookstore, applicants had to be enrolled full time, write an essay of no more than 250 words, and could receive the service only once ever.

events.title: The last Congress meeting of the autumn, with the banquet to follow
events.body: SGA's website announced on 30 November 2003 that the banquet would be held right after the next Congress meeting, which would also be the last Congress meeting of the autumn semester. That meeting, the fourteenth of the year, was called to order at 5:05 p.m. on 2 December 2003 with 25 of the 43 members present, and the vice president of public relations, Abby Lovan, told it that a picture would be taken for the yearbook at the banquet.

events.title: Robert Watkins elected first speaker of the senate on a disputed 9-8 vote
events.body: Congress elected Bowling Green sophomore Robert Watkins, who wrote the new constitution, as the first speaker of the senate by 9 votes to 8 over Brittany Fausey, with 17 of 20 members present voting. The result was immediately questioned because the new constitution was unclear on whether two-thirds of eligible voters or of total membership was required, and three members present were barred from voting under a judicial council ruling. Martin warned of a "semester of frustration" if the dispute was not settled at the year's final meeting. Fausey declined to challenge the result. SGA's own minutes date the vote to the 13 April meeting; the Herald's report ran two days later.

officers.name: Troy Ransdell

profile: Troy Ransdell chaired the SGA judicial council as chief justice in 2003-04, sworn in that September, and his term ran through both crises of the constitutional-convention year. When articles of impeachment were drafted against president-elect Nick Todd over the missing Dining Dollars funds in April 2004, Ransdell's council held that it could take no action on Todd's eligibility until there was more evidence and that the matter was the Congress's to decide, Ransdell describing the council as “a reactive body, not a proactive body” and noting another election would follow if Todd resigned. Days earlier he had flagged the ambiguity in the newly written constitution over the disputed election of Robert Watkins as speaker of the senate, saying it was unclear whether a two-thirds majority of the eligible voters or of all Congress members was required. officers.name: Josh Collins
officers.note: Sworn in as a Justice of the Judicial Council on 2 September 2003.
profile: Josh Collins, a junior from Jackson studying geography and Spanish, joined SGA in 2003 and was sworn in as a justice of the judicial council in September that year. When president-elect Nick Todd was accused in April 2004 of misusing more than $600 from the SGA Dining Dollars account, it was Collins who drafted the articles of impeachment against Todd's finance vice presidency, though the judicial council ruled a two-week impeachment could not be finished before Todd left that office anyway. Collins told the Herald the organisation would “be hearing echoes of this for a while.”

That March he had run for administrative vice president, campaigning on clarifying university policies for students and building a searchable database of past SGA legislation, and calling the previous autumn's rally against plus/minus grading “the clearest, most recent event that was SGA working, making our voices be heard.” He lost that race to Evelina Petkova, 692 votes to 481. In February 2005 the Herald reported that he and Katie Dawson had announced plans to run for SGA president; Dawson was elected that spring.

Previously chaired the Legislative Research committee, where he wrote and defended the new three-branch constitution (Bill 03-10-F). profile: Robert Watkins, a Bowling Green sophomore, was serving on Congress in October 2003 when he authored a resolution recommending students vote in the 4 November election, moving to suspend the by-laws so it could pass without the usual delay; it passed unanimously.

The following spring Watkins wrote the new three-branch constitution as chair of the Legislative Research Committee, and Congress elected him the senate's first speaker on 13 April 2004, defeating Brittany Fausey 9 votes to 8 with 17 of 20 members present. The result was disputed immediately because the new constitution did not make clear whether two-thirds of eligible voters or of the full membership was required, and three members present had been barred from voting by a judicial council ruling; one member warned of a “semester of frustration” if the dispute went unresolved. Abby Lovan had withdrawn from the race before the ballot, and Fausey declined to challenge the result.
Watkins went on to win the SGA presidency in April 2006 and served until his resignation that November; his full term is recorded under his leader entry for 2006-07.

leaders.name: Nick Todd
leaders.note: Elected SGA president in March 2004 with 772 of 1,232 votes and sworn in on 27 April, then resigned in July, citing personal conflicts within the association, after an investigation into money missing from an SGA Dining Dollars account. Executive vice president Katie Dawson acted as president until a special election in September, which Patti Johnson won unopposed. No plate on the Chambers wall carries his name; the 2004-05 plate reads Patti Johnson. Whether Todd ever took the student regent seat is not settled in the sources found so far.

profile: Nick Todd, a Henderson senior and SGA's outgoing vice president of finance, won the presidency in March 2004 with 772 of the 1,232 votes cast. Days before the new officers were sworn in on 27 April, the judicial council found $611 missing from the SGA Aramark Dining Dollars account, which had opened the year with $5,000. A senator drafted articles of impeachment against the finance post Todd was about to leave, and the council ruled a two-week process could not finish before he left it anyway. Only Todd, outgoing president John Bradley and the adviser held cards to the account.

He submitted his resignation in July, citing personal conflicts within the association. In May the university's internal auditor had reported more than $800 of questionable purchases from the account between August 2003 and May 2004, mostly small buys at campus restaurants with no receipts, and recommended he reimburse the money along with $71 charged on the SGA purchasing card after a spring break car rental. Campus police determined no police action was necessary. In September the dean of Student Life said Todd had been sanctioned by judicial affairs in July, disputing Todd's public account that losing the card was the only action taken against him.

Executive vice president Katie Dawson acted as president until the special election of 14 and 15 September. Patti Johnson, the previous year's executive vice president, was the only student to come forward for the office, saying she ran because of the turmoil within the organization, and was sworn in on 23 September. The Herald noted at the time that a re-election for SGA president is rare.

leaders.name: Katie Dawson
leaders.note: Filled the presidency through the summer of 2004. Dawson had run as Nick Todd's running mate in the March 2004 election and was executive vice president when he resigned in July; she acted as president until the special election of 14 and 15 September, which Patti Johnson won unopposed. No source found says she was sworn in. The Herald reported both of that year's swearings-in, Todd's at the April banquet and Johnson's at the September reception, and described Dawson only as acting president, which is how this site records her. She is counted among the presidents all the same, because she held the office: the rule here is that holding it counts, however briefly and by whatever route. She was elected president in her own right the following spring and is on the Chambers wall for 2005-06 only, so the plaque does not record this stretch. The student regent seat did not pass to her.

sources.label: Herald, 24 Aug 2004 - Todd cites personal conflicts in resignation
Herald, 2 Sep 2004 - SGA preparing for September elections

profile: Katie Dawson held the SGA presidency for about two months in the summer of 2004 without having been elected to it. She had come up through the cabinet as Nick Todd's running mate in the March election and was his executive vice president when he resigned in July amid the Dining Dollars investigation. She acted in the office until students voted in a special election that September.

Hers is the only one of the archive's four mid-year vacancies filled this way. In 2004 the presidency was treated as vacant and put back to the students, with the executive vice president acting until they had voted. When Rob Watkins resigned in November 2006 and when Johnathon Boles resigned in January 2009, the executive vice president succeeded to the office instead, Jeanne Johnson being sworn in as president at that year's Winter Banquet. The same organisation met the same kind of vacancy in two different ways within five years.
She was elected president in her own right for 2005-06, and the Chambers wall carries her for that year alone.

leaders.name: Patti Johnson
leaders.note: Confirmed: president-elect Nick Todd resigned in July 2004 amid a dining-funds investigation; Johnson, who had been executive vice president the year before, ran unopposed in the September 2004 special election and was sworn in Sept. 23, matching the plaque year. A Board of Regents resolution read into the 22 Jul 2005 minutes confirms she served as the board's student member from August 2004 to July 2005, when Katie Dawson was sworn in to replace her.

sources.label: WKU Board of Regents minutes, 22 Jul 2005 (TopSCHOLAR)

profile: Patti Johnson, a senior from Marion, had been active in SGA for over three years and served on committees including public relations and athletics before becoming executive vice president in 2003-04. Nick Todd, the vice president of finance, was elected president for 2004-05 in March 2004, but before the new officers were sworn in on April 27, SGA's judicial council fielded an allegation that $611 was missing from the SGA Dining Dollars account, an account that had started the year with $5,000. Senator Josh Collins drafted articles of impeachment against Todd's vice presidency, but the judicial council ruled a two-week impeachment process could not finish before he left that office anyway. Johnson had not planned to run for president herself, but after Todd's resignation that July she entered the September 2004 special election as the only candidate to show interest, saying she stayed on because of "the turmoil within the organization" and that she knew "what it takes to get the job done."

Johnson ran unopposed for president and student regent in the Sept. 14-15 online election, the group having been without an elected president since July. She said she was disappointed that students would not "really get to make a decision," but still planned light campaigning, and she wanted to continue reviewing the plus/minus grading proposal and to make faculty evaluations available to students.

Johnson received 1,291 votes in the two-day uncontested election and was sworn in as president at SGA's fall reception on Sept. 23, 2004, one week after her election. She said committees had been formed and members had begun proposing legislation, and she looked forward to being sworn in as student regent at the Oct. 29 Board of Regents meeting, declaring it was "back to business." She served through the year until Katie Dawson was elected to succeed her in the March 2005 spring election.

Johnson served as the Board of Regents' student member from August 2004 to July 2005, a term confirmed by the resolution of appreciation the board read into its July 22, 2005 minutes when Katie Dawson, the executive vice president who had served alongside her all year, was sworn in to replace her. Dawson had come up through the cabinet as Todd's running mate in the original March 2004 election and had acted as interim president during the summer vacancy before Johnson's win.

events.title: Internal audit recommended Todd repay SGA money
events.body: WKU's Office of the Internal Auditor reported in May that $872 in questionable purchases had been made from the SGA Dining Dollars account between August 2003 and May 2004, mostly small buys at campus restaurants with no receipts. The report recommended that Nick Todd reimburse the money, plus $71 for a charge made with the SGA purchasing card after a spring break car rental. Campus police determined that no police action was necessary.

events.title: Patti Johnson emerged as the only candidate in the special election
events.body: Roughly 13 students, ranging from freshmen to fifth-year seniors, met on Tuesday to discuss the organization and September's special elections. Marion senior Patti Johnson, the previous year's executive vice president, was the only student to show interest in the presidency, and said she decided to run because of "the turmoil within the organization." Applications were also taken for the 23 open senate seats ahead of online voting on Sept. 14-15.

events.title: Dean of Student Life contradicted Todd on sanctions
events.body: Howard Bailey, dean of Student Life, said Todd had been sanctioned by judicial affairs in July over the alleged misuse of university funds, disputing Todd's public claim that losing access to the Dining Dollars card was the only action taken against him. Bailey said federal privacy law barred him from revealing the sanctions. Todd acknowledged he was also no longer allowed to handle any SGA funds.

events.title: SGA approved a $110,000 budget
events.body: SGA approved a $110,000 budget for the 2004-05 academic year, up from $105,000 the year before, despite earlier expectations of a $15,000 to $17,000 cut under the university's budget reduction plan. Most of the money went toward operating fees, campus improvements and organizational aid. Adviser Charley Pride credited steady enrollment growth for the increase.

events.title: Johnson sworn in as president after winning 1,291 votes
events.body: Patti Johnson was sworn in as SGA president at the organization's fall reception on Sept. 23, after receiving 1,291 votes in the uncontested online election held Sept. 14 and 15. The 23 new senators were seated in the first fall senate election held under SGA's new constitution. Johnson was due to be sworn in as student regent at the Oct. 29 Board of Regents meeting.

events.title: SGA proposed a faculty evaluation pilot to the University Senate
events.body: SGA prepared to propose a two-year pilot program to the University Senate that would add five questions on matters such as office hours, punctuality and textbook use to faculty evaluations and post the answers on TopNet for students. Senator Josh Collins wrote the proposal with Troy Ransdell and Morgan Phelps after SGA scaled back an earlier push to release entire evaluations. The questions could appear on evaluations at the end of spring 2005 if the study was approved.

events.title: Katie Dawson elected SGA president for 2005-06
events.body: Executive Vice President Katie Dawson defeated Senate Speaker Josh Collins 1,268 to 472 in the spring election's only contested race to become the next SGA president. Students also passed a package of 40 constitutional amendments 1,193 to 262 and voted 1,019 to 669 to ask the Board of Regents to institute a $9 per semester Talisman yearbook fee. Mason Stevenson and Melissa Paris won the two vice presidencies unopposed, and all 25 senate candidates on the ballot were elected.

events.title: SGA funded the Buy-A-Book program
events.body: SGA passed legislation 22-2 on April 5 allocating $2,000 to the Buy-A-Book program, and the University Bookstore pledged to match the amount. The bill by senator Katharine Pettit was amended unanimously to help 20 students who needed financial assistance buying textbooks instead of 10. Recipients were to be chosen by the academic affairs committee based on a required essay and need.

events.title: Goodrum found not guilty in Katie Autry murder trial
events.body: A jury in Owensboro found Lucas Goodrum, 23, of Scottsville not guilty of the May 2003 murder of Pellville freshman Melissa "Katie" Autry, who was set on fire in her Poland Hall dorm room and died three days later. The verdict came March 21 after three hours of deliberation, ending a three-week trial that had been moved from Warren County. Stephen Soules had earlier pleaded guilty to murder, rape, sodomy, arson and robbery and expected life in prison.

events.title: SGA judicial council fielded impeachment bid against president-elect Todd
events.body: Days before new officers were due to be sworn in on April 27, SGA's judicial council found that $611 was missing from the SGA Aramark Dining Dollars account, which had started the academic year with $5,000 and had about $1,200 left. Senator Josh Collins drafted articles of impeachment against Todd's outgoing vice presidency of finance, but the council ruled a two-week impeachment process could not be completed before he left that office regardless. Only Todd, outgoing president John Bradley and adviser Charley Pride held cards to the account.

events.title: SGA sets online special election for September
events.body: SGA scheduled an online presidential election for Sept. 14-15 to replace the candidate elected president in March. Students who had cast ballots for president the previous spring were asked to vote again.

events.title: Campus reaction to re-election divided
events.body: The Herald reported that reactions on campus to the Dining Dollars investigation and Todd's resignation varied, noting that a re-election for SGA president is rare. Bowling Green sophomore Alex Hall said he had voted for Todd in the March election.

events.title: Former SGA officers write to rebut Todd
events.body: Western alumni who had held SGA office wrote to the Herald objecting to Nick Todd's remarks in the Aug. 24 issue. The writers, who had served with Todd in SGA, said they were dismayed by his lack of integrity in the matter.

events.title: Big Red Card debit proposal put to SGA
events.body: A proposal to create new student identification cards that would also serve as debit cards was presented to SGA for approval earlier in the month. Auxiliary Services Director Rob Chrisler described the proposal to the Herald.

events.title: Dialogue Day put deans in the coffee shop
events.body: SGA held Dialogue Day at Java City in Helm Library on 4 November 2004, an open forum where students could raise any topic with university administrators. More than 20 students and seven administrators took part, among them Gene Tice, vice president for student affairs and campus services, and Bob Reber, associate dean of the Gordon Ford College of Business. SGA paid for refreshments; executive vice president Katie Dawson said the point was to get names attached to faces so students would feel less intimidated about making appointments.
events.money: SGA funded refreshments through legislation co-written by senator Tim Howard

events.title: Dialogue Day announced as a decade-old idea revived
events.body: The Herald reported on 28 October 2004 that SGA would hold Dialogue Day from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on 4 November at Java City. Senator Jessica Martin said students could go through an entire college career without meeting their dean. Dawson said the programme had been an SGA idea a decade earlier but had only run regularly for the previous three years.

events.title: SGA funded a recycling centre in Downing University Center
events.body: On 8 February 2005 the senate passed legislation paying for a recycling centre in DUC and eight new benches near the dorms. Campus services manager Greg Fear said the centre would be three heavy-duty bins taking plastic, aluminium and paper, replacing cheaper dorm bins that students had destroyed six years earlier. The bins were to cost about $2,000 from the campus improvements committee budget.
events.money: about $2,000 from the campus improvements committee budget

src.label: College Heights Herald 80:34, 10 Feb 2005 - "SGA votes to add recycling center in DUC" (TopSCHOLAR)

events.title: Provide-A-Ride extended to Thursday nights
events.body: SGA, the university Parking and Transportation Committee and Yellow Cab agreed to extend the free late-night Provide-A-Ride service to Thursdays from the first week of classes in autumn 2005. A single 15-passenger van ran 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. Thursday through Saturday, free with a WKU ID and $2 without, at a cost to the university of about $150 a night. The new one-year contract also covered rides 30 minutes before and 90 minutes into home football games. President Patti Johnson said Thursday was as busy as Friday and Saturday.

events.title: Campus Cleanup Day handed out green T-shirts and free food
events.body: SGA ran its Campus Cleanup Day on 18 April 2005, with volunteers meeting in front of Cherry Hall and splitting into teams assigned to sections of campus. Senators had unanimously voted $1,000 from the campus improvements budget on 1 March for green "Cleaning up the Hill" T-shirts, and about $500 from the Aramark budget for food at the Campus Engagement Day reception that followed on South Lawn. Facilities management donated 300 pairs of gloves and 200 trash bags.
events.money: $1,000 for T-shirts plus about $500 for the reception

events.title: Senate spent $12,000 in under twenty minutes
events.body: On 19 April 2005 SGA senators applauded after spending more than $12,000 in fewer than twenty minutes at the end of the budget year. The purchases included bicycle racks, an emergency phone for the community college, about 1,000 red towels for promotional events at $2,000 from the public relations budget, and up to $115 for 2,500 bookmarks advertising tutorial and educational assistance programmes. About $35,000 was still unspent, and president-elect Katie Dawson was to distribute it over the summer before the university reclaimed it.

events.title: Nick Todd resigns the presidency
events.body: Nick Todd, a Henderson senior elected in March with 772 of the 1,232 votes cast, submitted his resignation as SGA president in July 2004, citing personal conflicts within the association. The former vice president of finance had come under investigation in April over the misuse of more than $600 from an SGA Dining Dollars account. Executive vice president Katie Dawson acted as president until a new election, set for 14 and 15 September. The Herald reported the resignation when students returned, on 24 August.

profile: Evelina Petkova, a junior from Sofia, Bulgaria, ran for administrative vice president in March 2004 after three years in SGA, beginning as secretary of the public relations committee and chairing it in 2003-04. Other candidates that spring pledged continued opposition to plus/minus grading, but Petkova's own remarks focused on making the grading pilot the academic quality committee had proposed work well for students, and on improving communication between SGA's officers and its new legislative branch, telling the Herald “the administrators don’t listen to the students’ opinions, which is very disappointing.”

Petkova defeated Josh Collins 692 votes to 481 in the March 2004 election, alongside Nick Todd's win for president. In office for 2004-05, she sat on SGA's Executive Board and the WKU Budget Council, and was recorded as the first international student to serve on the SGA executive board.

profile: Jessica Martin, a junior from Bulan, ran for SGA president in March 2004 while serving as vice president of administration, having chaired Academic Affairs and served as vice-chair of Constitutional Review earlier in her SGA career. At a candidates' debate that month she argued that programs the university had proposed but not implemented could be frozen, and that money being saved for later should be spent while it was still available. She lost to Nick Todd, 772 votes to 424.

After Todd resigned that July amid a Dining Dollars spending investigation and Katie Dawson took over as acting president, Martin was still involved enough that fall to report application numbers for the vacant presidency and the senate's open seats at the September organizing meeting. When Patti Johnson won that election, Martin became chief of staff under her.

profile: Dawson served as both SGA president and student regent during Western's centennial year. When the university launched its 14-month centennial celebration on Nov. 19, 2005, she spoke at the dedication of Centennial Plaza, offering her own meaning for the school slogan: "Find what you love and carry it with you your whole life through."

Her spring semester was dominated by a proposed $46-per-semester fee for three campus construction projects. At a student forum with President Gary Ransdell she suggested exempting the next year's seniors, who would graduate before any project was finished; the Board of Regents rejected the exemption 10-1 at its April 7 meeting and approved the fee 9-1. Dawson cast the lone abstention, saying that although she supported the fee, she could not vote for it with so many seniors counting on the exemption.

Her term ended at Western's 159th commencement on May 13, 2006, where the Radcliff native graduated with a degree in corporate and organizational communication and addressed her 1,797 fellow undergraduates as SGA president. She charged the graduates to have courage, endurance, strength, patience and character, saying success was knowing "when to throw in the towel and when to wave it around and cheer."

events.title: The plus/minus grading fight
events.body: An Institutional Research report on plus and minus grading, a protest broadside, a post-winter-term student survey and an SGA handbook all survive - one of the few academic-policy campaigns documented from research through to public agitation.

events.title: SGA passed less legislation in the fall than usual
events.body: The Herald reported that SGA had approved less legislation in the fall semester than in previous years, without stating a count. The same issue reported that Jeanne Johnson had been elected the new speaker of the senate.

events.title: SGA took up a proposed $45 construction fee
events.body: At its first regular meeting of the spring semester, SGA discussed a proposed $45-per-semester fee to pay for a campus-wide wireless network, a new health center and renovations to the Ivan Wilson Center for Fine Arts. President Katie Dawson supported the fee, and Western's chief financial officer estimated it would raise about $1.4 million a year.

events.title: Ransdell asked SGA for a resolution backing the fee
events.body: WKU President Gary Ransdell came to the SGA meeting and urged senators to pass a resolution supporting the proposed $45 fee, which the Board of Regents would vote on April 7. Dawson sat on that board as student regent, and SGA officers said a supporting resolution was likely within a few weeks.

events.title: Executive vice president aired an internal rift
events.body: Executive Vice President Mason Stevenson read a letter at the SGA meeting saying some members trying to protect their political interests had "thwarted" SGA's mission to improve Western. The letter outlined his concerns about relations between the executive and legislative branches.

src.label: Herald 81:33, 2 Mar 2006, "VP of Student Government Association: We’ve Got Problems"

events.title: Senate put $2,000 toward SGA's 40th anniversary party
events.body: The Herald reported that SGA planned a campus-wide party to mark four decades of student government at Western. Only the headline of that report survives in the archive, so what the senate voted and spent on the party is not recorded here.

src.label: Herald 81:37, 16 Mar 2006, "Student Government Association Plans Anniversary Party"

events.title: Regents approved the fee; Dawson's senior exemption failed
events.body: The Board of Regents voted 9-1 to approve the $46-per-semester construction fee, with Dawson abstaining, and rejected 10-1 her proposal to exempt next year's seniors, an idea she had raised at a student forum the week before. Dawson said that although she supported the fee, she could not vote for it with so many seniors counting on the exemption.

events.title: Rob Watkins elected SGA president
events.body: Bowling Green senior Robert Watkins won the online election for SGA president after spending more than a week seeking supporters who would vote on TopNet. He defeated Berea junior Kara Ratliff, and the results were announced Tuesday at a crowded Revolution 91.

src.label: Herald 81:42, 13 Apr 2006, "See Rob Run, Win . . . Barely"

events.title: Executive board issued its first veto of the year
events.body: After the Tuesday senate meeting, the SGA executive board vetoed a bill that would have financed community- and campus-oriented projects through civic engagement grants, the first time it exercised its veto power that year. The Herald reported the grants were "a reality for only about 30 minutes" and that time restraints halted an appeal of the veto.

src.label: Herald 81:44, 20 Apr 2006, "Time Restraints Halt Veto Appeal"

events.title: Herald editorial attacked SGA misspending
events.body: A Herald editorial titled "SGA misspending" said members should not have to be "motivated by a giveaway to show up for meetings." It noted that the opinion page had devoted considerable space in recent weeks to both positive and negative aspects of SGA, which it said could and should be an important organization on campus.

events.title: WKU launched its centennial celebration
events.body: Western kicked off a 14-month celebration of its 1906 founding on Saturday, Nov. 19, dedicating three new campus landmarks including Centennial Plaza. SGA President Katie Dawson spoke at the plaza dedication, offering her own meaning of the school slogan "The Spirit Makes the Master."

events.title: Civic engagement bracelets and Katrina relief opened the year
events.body: The earliest 2005-06 meeting in the SGA collection, on 6 September 2005, was convened to discuss elections, the retreat, Hurricane Katrina and Civic Engagement bracelets. The bracelets appear again in the minutes of 20 September and 1 November 2005.

events.title: Campus Safety Walk and Provide-A-Ride carried into a new year
events.body: At its second meeting of the autumn the senate discussed the retreat, the Campus Safety Walk, the athletics committee and Provide-A-Ride. Provide-A-Ride appears again in the minutes of 4 October 2005.

events.title: SGA screened Living with Cancer and began a documentary series
events.body: The senate discussed the Living with Cancer documentary at its meeting of 11 October 2005, alongside Listen Up Legislators, homecoming and Dialogue Day. An SGA documentary is recorded in the minutes of 4 and 18 October and a documentary series in those of 25 October.

events.title: Dialogue Day put students in a room with administrators
events.body: Dialogue Day appears in three consecutive sets of senate minutes in October 2005 as a programme SGA was organising, alongside the documentary series and Listen Up Legislators. SGA returned to it the following year in Resolution 03-06-F of 2 October 2006, catalogued as proposing a day for students to meet administrators.

events.title: SGA organised a forum for transfer students
events.body: The 25 October 2005 senate meeting covered Dialogue Day, the documentary series, Listen Up Legislators and a transfer student forum. The forum recurs in the minutes of 8 November and 29 November 2005 and 14 February 2006, making it a sustained programme rather than a single evening.

events.title: Senate took up library hours for finals week
events.body: At its last meeting of the autumn semester the senate discussed the banquet, library hours for finals week, and legislation. Extended library hours during finals became a recurring SGA concern; a bill of April 2007 proposed SGA funding for them.

events.title: Senators moved to censure President Katie Dawson
events.body: The Herald of 7 March 2006 reported that SGA senators would ask the Judicial Council to censure President Katie Dawson. The same issue carried two opinion pieces on the organisation, one asking whether student government was missing in action and one arguing it should be improved. The archive records no outcome to the censure move beyond its delay two days later.

events.title: Senators delayed the censure decision
events.body: Two days after the move became public the Herald reported that SGA senators had delayed a decision on censuring President Katie Dawson. No later issue in the digitised run records the matter being resolved.

events.title: Campus Cleanup ran on 9 March 2006
events.body: The senate had discussed campus cleanup at its 7 March 2006 meeting, and the Herald of 9 March carried the item Campus CleanUp Today, reporting the event as happening that day rather than announcing it in advance. SGA's own website later said the clean-up traced its roots to Henry Hardin Cherry's presidency and that SGA sponsored it each year.

events.title: Senate weighed an education funding rally and an SGA archivist
events.body: The 7 March 2006 senate meeting covered a Why Kentucky Education is Important rally, the campus cleanup, and the creation of an archivist position within SGA.

events.title: Presidential candidates agreed on most issues at the spring forum
events.body: The senate had scheduled a presidential debate at its 28 March 2006 meeting, and the Herald of 4 April reported that the SGA candidates agreed on many issues. The same issue reported that seniors might be exempted from the new $46 student fee.

events.title: SGA still had $30,000 unspent with two weeks of term left
events.body: The Herald of 2 May 2006 reported that the SGA budget had $30,000 remaining. The same issue carried a column arguing the Herald was not responsible for the lack of enthusiasm for student government on campus.

executive.name: Mason Stevenson
executive.note: Read a letter to the March 2006 SGA meeting airing a rift between the executive and legislative branches.
profile: Mason Stevenson, a Princeton junior double-majoring in broadcasting and political science, joined SGA as parliamentarian in fall 2003, a non-voting post he said taught him parliamentary procedure; he had previously served as treasurer of the Southwest Hall Council and was a resident assistant at Bemis Lawrence Hall, and had earlier helped start a College Republicans chapter at Paducah Community College. He ran for one of the new senate's elected seats that March, saying he wanted a vote in decisions rather than the parliamentarian's advisory role, and won; that fall he chaired the senate's Legislative Research Committee.

In March 2005 Stevenson and Melissa Paris were elected to SGA's two vice presidencies unopposed, alongside Katie Dawson's contested win for president. As executive vice president in 2005-06, he read a letter to the 2 March 2006 SGA meeting airing a rift between the executive and legislative branches, saying some members protecting their own political interests had “thwarted” the organization's mission to improve Western; the Herald headlined its report “We’ve Got Problems.”

executive.note: Secretary of the Senate before winning the administrative vice presidency unopposed, in the same uncontested slate as Mason Stevenson's win as executive vice president. She held the budget rather than a vice presidency of unstated portfolio as this archive once recorded: she distributed the SGA budget to senators, ran the Organizational Aid interest meeting and application process, and sat on the WKU Budget Council. The minutes give her title as Administrative Vice-President from the first meeting of the year.
profile: Melissa Paris, a sophomore double-majoring in political science and English and a Barnes-Campbell Hall council member, sat on SGA's Legislative Research Committee when she ran for one of the new senate's elected seats in March 2004. She said raising student awareness was her biggest issue, and that the plus/minus grading pilot mattered to her because she believed the administration meant to fold it into GPAs within two years; she was elected.

In March 2005 Paris was elected, alongside Mason Stevenson, to SGA's two vice presidencies unopposed. The senate's own minutes give her title as administrative vice president from the first meeting of 2005-06; she distributed the SGA budget to senators, ran the Organizational Aid interest meeting and application process, and sat on the WKU Budget Council.

profile: Katharine Pettit, a freshman from Elkton, said her own standing as a newcomer to the Hill would help her voice other new students' concerns when she ran for one of the new senate's elected seats in March 2004. She opposed plus/minus grading and sat that spring on the Legislative Review Committee, checking proposed bills against the new constitution before they reached the floor. She was elected.

Pettit was confirmed Director of Academic and Student Affairs at SGA's first meeting of 2005-06, on 6 September 2005, and asked senators to bring student issues to their committees; the office was reported vacant at the 31 January 2006 meeting. She returned to SGA's judicial branch and was reappointed an associate justice of the Judicial Council on 5 September 2006, having served in that post the previous year after leaving the directorship.

profile: Jedediah “Eli” Conrad ran in the Student Government Association's spring 2005 elections, one of the candidates named in the Herald's special election issue of 15 March 2005 alongside Emily Lovan and Ricky Jordan. He was elected Speaker of the Senate for 2005-06 and presided from the chamber's first meeting, setting a Friday 5 p.m. deadline for legislation to make the week's agenda. He resigned at the meeting of 6 December 2005, citing conflicts with his class schedule.

He continued writing for the Herald's opinion pages after leaving office: a letter headlined “Student Government Association Should Be Improved” ran 7 March 2006, and another, “Herald Staff Is a Loaded Gun,” the following month.

leaders.name: Robert Watkins
leaders.note: Single-year plate and the only name attached to 2006 because Watkins resigned partway through the 2006-07 term; no plate covers the full year. Confirmed against Herald election coverage: a Bowling Green senior, he won the SGA presidency in the 13 April 2006 online election, defeating Berea junior Kara Ratliff. He had been elected the first speaker of the senate under the new constitution on 15 April 2004, a result contested 9-8 and then upheld. He resigned as president and student regent on 28 November 2006, per SGA's own senate minutes for that day's regularly scheduled Tuesday meeting, which record the resignation being read into the record; this site previously followed a Herald account giving the date as 30 November, which this run corrects against the primary minutes.
